### 3.2 R2. How has studies on GenAI for K-12 education been designed and implemented?

This section presents the design approaches employed in the study, including the measures used by the researchers, which directly connect to the learning outcomes of those studies. Examples of learning activities performed by the researchers and/or instructors are provided to illustrate how some of the activities were carried out, along with their recommendations for future research.

#### 3.2.1 Study design

The study design uncovered in this review pertains to the design approaches adopted by the reviewed studies. The measures used in these studies were also collected. It is important to highlight the design process of the identified studies to understand the procedures involved in learning with ChatGPT, as well as the elements measured during the teaching and learning process.

#### 3.2.2 Design approach

Based on the reviewed papers, 9 out of 30 (30%) utilized a quasi-experimental approach to implement their ideas of GenAI in the classroom. As illustrated in [Figure 7](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/education/articles/10.3389/feduc.2025.1647573/full#fig7), papers employing descriptive and mixed-method approaches each accounted for 20% of the analyzed data, while exploratory and case study approaches each represented 10% of the selected works. Additionally, one paper each used experimental, action research, or qualitative research approaches. All these methodologies are valuable and complement each other, providing comprehensive insights into the functionalities of GenAI for teaching and learning.

Figure 7

#### 3.2.3 Measures

Researchers are interested in various measures to understand the feasibility of GenAI in classrooms for teaching and learning. These measures, primarily psychological variables, include attitudes toward AI and creativity, cognitive trust, affective trust, perceptions of usability, and continuance intention to use (); self-regulation progress using motivation, engagement, and self-efficacy as indicators (); trust, technology acceptance, and satisfaction with ChatGPT explanations (); self-regulated learning (); critical thinking and problem-solving (); scientific inquiry interaction with an AI inquiry assistant (); computational thinking and problem-solving skills (); higher-order thinking (); problem-solving and task completion (); and flow experience, self-efficacy, and learning achievement (). We identified only two studies that specifically consider how GenAI supports self-regulated learning.

Aside from surveys and interviews using these psychological variables, the studies do not consider objective measures of student learning outcomes, such as standardized tests or quizzes. These measures provide insight into the outcomes resulting from exploring GenAI in teaching and learning settings. For instance, found that using ChatGPT in their experimental design study reported lower levels of flow experience, self-efficacy, and learning achievement compared to those utilizing conventional methods.

#### 3.2.4 Learning activities and experience

As previously mentioned, each of the identified papers focuses on specific ideas and demonstrates how GenAI can be used to teach those concepts. While not all the papers provide detailed walkthroughs of the processes, some of the activities presented in the literature can be helpful for teaching and learning with GenAI by following existing examples. For instance, used “Sustainable Energy” as a collaborative learning project, where participants utilized various generative AI tools to collect data and organize knowledge. found that structuring high school physics class content to incorporate ChatGPT for analyzing experimental data helped students analyze data and solve problems.

An example of an intervention study is provided by . The project, conducted in a middle school context, consisted of a series of three workshops, each lasting 3 hours and held over the course of 3 weeks. The educational strategy was designed to introduce students to artificial intelligence (AI) through three distinct perspectives. The third workshop focused on generative AI. It began with an overview of image recognition systems, explaining how web scrapers collect image-text pairs to train large-scale models. These datasets, originally intended for recognition tasks, also serve as the foundation for text-to-image generation. A popular generative AI tool, Midjourney, was used to demonstrate this capability. Students were introduced to the basics of prompt crafting and shown visual examples of prompts alongside the images generated by Midjourney. Following this, students were divided into small teams and provided with computers to collaboratively explore and experiment with the tool, allowing them to engage hands-on with generative AI concepts.

Generally, most studies do not detail the learning activities in which GenAI has been used. It is important to present these details to serve as resources for other researchers or practitioners to adopt in their classrooms or courses. To avoid redundancy, this paper has not detailed the GenAI activities reported in the reviewed studies. Instead, it highlights each of the primary studies, making it easier for other researchers to identify which papers to consult for specific content areas or topics they are interested in using GenAI to facilitate.

#### 3.2.5 Recommendations

Nearly all the reviewed papers (90%) emphasize the need for teachers’ professional development for AI-integrated classrooms (e.g., ; ). These papers highlight the importance of developing instructional approaches to build substantial understanding and experience with subject-specific AI applications through authentic learning tasks and fostering AI literacy (). In addition to teacher learning opportunities, assessing learning outcomes before and after engaging with ChatGPT () is recommended. suggest investigating the cognitive and emotional experiences of both researchers and teachers using large language models for teacher learning purposes. emphasize examining the impact of student-GenAI partnerships on learning and investigating these partnerships’ effects on various learning outcomes in diverse settings.

Future research should explore not only the direct, short-term impacts of GenAI but also its indirect and long-term effects on creativity and critical thinking across different domains (). Researchers also note the benefit of conducting pre-tests to better gauge the effectiveness of GenAI intervention initiatives (). call for longitudinal studies on the topic, including research-based evidence about generative AI’s role and impacts on pupils’ learning outcomes, especially when learning material has been adapted with GenAI. Based on study results, they suggest that educational GAI platforms should support customizable teacher-in-the-loop systems to enhance the trustworthiness and content-focus of GAI systems. Experimenting with various GenAI tools may be necessary due to the occasional inaccuracies of GPT-3.5’s responses () and the evolution of GPT and GenAI tools.

## 4 Discussion

GenAI has arrived, and its implications for teaching and learning, including K-12 education, cannot be overstated. K-12 education lays the foundation for future education and career success by preparing students with the knowledge, skills, and confidence needed for college and careers. It is crucial to support this demographic with emerging technologies and opportunities to ensure they are future-ready citizens. To provide timely insights into how GenAI is being used to enhance teaching and learning in K-12 settings, this paper reviews empirical and primary studies on the adoption of GenAI across the K-12 context. This article offers a window into the GenAI for K-12 world, showcasing how researchers, K-12 educators, and practitioners have used GenAI in their instructional practices, which is valuable in addressing the question of how GenAI can be effectively integrated into the school system. This section further highlights and discusses the main findings from the reviewed papers.

### 4.1 Characteristics of educational level

Based on the 30 selected papers, none focused on early childhood education (ECE). The papers that were identified but did not meet the inclusion criteria evaluated the integration of AI-supported ChatGPT into ECE STEM education from the teachers’ perspective (; ). Although Uğraş et al.’s work involved training 18 teachers on the use of ChatGPT, there was no evaluation of the effectiveness of the instructional exercise or how the pupils benefited from learning with the GenAI tool. Su and Yang also explored teachers’ views to understand the potential benefits and challenges of using ChatGPT in early childhood education. More research is needed within the ECE context to provide insights into how GenAI can improve pupils’ learning and teachers’ teaching.

### 4.2 Parental involvement in learning with GenAI

Our results show that only one paper () considers parents in exploring GenAI use for learning. The study included parents as part of the research demographic, which also comprised teachers and students. Parental involvement in students’ learning has been considered valuable. observed the role of parents as a factor influencing learning and development in computing-related subjects. Oyedoyin et al.’s observation aligns with prior studies highlighting the importance of parental involvement in eradicating ICT illiteracy and increasing educational equality (), as well as how parental involvement in their children’s learning positively affects learners’ motivation, attitude, and academic achievement (). Given the value of parental involvement in learning, more research should explore the use of GenAI with parents and their children.

### 4.3 Teachers’ use of GenAI

In this review, only one paper focused on how teachers have implemented GenAI in practice and evaluated its use. Prior works (e.g., ) aimed to integrate GenAI into elementary literacy education by prompting ChatGPT to generate high-quality questions during a read-aloud. While Yang et al.’s study holds implications for GenAI in schools, evaluating the activities and how they enhance teaching and learning is important. The author opines that GenAI facilitates teaching and learning and can be a powerful support for teachers, but agency and decision-making must remain with the teacher. asserts that unless prompted, GenAI does not know the students, backgrounds, and cultural context, making the teacher critical in implementing teaching and learning with GenAI tools. interesting contribution also reported from the teacher’s perspective the learning activities that can foster self-regulated learning (SRL) processes and self-determination theory (SDT) needs. However, how these activities support SRL and SDT in practice remains unseen. While it is a consensus that the use of any technological tool relies on teachers’ expertise and initiatives, there is a need for experimenting and evidence of real-time use of GenAI tools within the school level.

### 4.4 Use of GenAI in different subject domains

As shown in the findings section, GenAI has been utilized in various subject domains, predominantly within STEM fields in the K-12 context. For instance, explore physics educators’ perceptions of the educational use of ChatGPT and future changes in society and the educational environment. Beyond the identified subject domains, there is a growing effort to utilize GenAI across disciplines. Researchers have explored the transformative potential of GenAI in geography education, focusing on its impacts on curriculum, pedagogy, and assessment through the lens of the SAMR (Substitution, Augmentation, Modification, and Redefinition) model. Evaluating the effectiveness of metrics or hypothesized approaches is needed. discuss how GenAI can be integrated into chemistry education using the TPACK framework and prompt engineering, emphasizing the types of knowledge teachers need to apply GAI effectively and the need to further develop theoretical frameworks for teachers’ knowledge in the age of GAI. also discusses the possibilities of GenAI use in drama education. It is evident that GenAI has implications for all disciplines, regardless of their focus. However, detailed reports or real-time use and evaluation of its usability based on defined metrics are necessary to affirm most of the conceptual and position papers on the subject. Overall, our findings indicate that more work is required on the use of AI across multiple subject domains within the K-12 context.

### 4.5 Design and implementation

It is interesting to note that most of the identified studies utilized a quasi-experimental approach in designing their research. This approach allowed researchers to measure the impact of their intervention and ascertain the effectiveness of GenAI use over traditional methods or other alternatives. More research using true experimental designs is necessary. Experimental research is considered a powerful tool for establishing causal relationships between educational interventions and student outcomes, allowing researchers to test the effectiveness of new teaching methods or programs by randomly assigning students to control and experimental groups. In measuring students’ knowledge and learning with GenAI, the majority of studies have designed and developed self-reported questionnaires to assess their learning and understanding using self-perceptions, which may not be accurate measures. Future work should consider objective measures such as test items. Using self-reported measures in research such as surveys or interviews can limit both the validity and generalizability of findings compared to objective measures like standardized tests. Self-reports are vulnerable to biases such as social desirability and inaccurate recall, which can distort the data and threaten construct validity, the extent to which a tool accurately measures the intended concept (). Additionally, variability in how individuals interpret questions can introduce measurement error, reducing internal validity (). From a generalizability standpoint, self-reports may not perform consistently across different populations or cultural contexts, limiting external validity. For example, cultural norms can influence how people report emotions or behaviors, making it difficult to apply findings broadly (). In contrast, objective measures offer standardized, replicable data that are less prone to individual interpretation, enhancing both the reliability and validity of research outcomes ().

Additionally, the activities implemented in research studies on how GenAI supports teaching and learning in the classroom should ensure scalability. assert that without sensible AI use guidelines, AI is likely to have a net-negative effect on learning based on trials with ChatGPT on various cognitive tasks organized around Bloom’s Taxonomy of learning. Valcea et al.’s exposition further shows the need for more trials to understand how AI tools can be effectively used to enhance learning. Researchers have reported a dearth of published work on detailed reports of GenAI use within normal school curriculum contents and its testing with pupils in the real learning context of school classes (). Nevertheless, there are some efforts in this regard, conducting research with school pupils and populations within the K-12 context. This study reports on the synthesized work produced by researchers and practitioners attempting to enhance their teaching and students’ learning using different GenAI tools.

### 4.6 Study limitations and future research

There are other GenAI tools that were not covered in our search terms, which may have been explored by researchers or practitioners. For instance, Microsoft Bing, Google Bard, Adobe Firefly, Education Copilot, Khanmigo, Magic AI, Midjourney, Research Rabbit, and SlidesAI. Future research should explore these tools or other commercial or open-source GenAI tools available to understand how they can be effectively integrated into the classroom. Our study shows that a few GenAI tools (such as ChatGPT and Copilot) are primarily implemented with different education stakeholders despite the numerous tools available. Future research could explore and compare different tools to provide insights into how these tools could enhance teaching and learning. With clear evidence from our review and researchers’ submissions (e.g., ) of limited research experimenting with GenAI tools by teachers and students in school or out-of-school settings, there is a need for high-quality research and intervention studies along these lines. Our research only considers papers published in English, which implies that valuable findings from papers published in other prominent languages like Arabic, French, and Spanish may be missing. This review notes a lack of studies from Africa, the Middle East, and South America from the selected papers. Only English-language publications meets the inclusion criteria. As a result of these geographic and linguistic limitations, the author of this work acknowledges the potential of how these factors might bias the synthesis or exclude potentially important findings from non-English speaking regions or different educational contexts. While the papers reviewed in this study are limited to 30, they provide useful insights into how GenAI can be integrated within the K-12 system. Fewer papers have been used to perform systematic reviews in previous research. For instance, synthesize findings from 13 papers. However, future work should consider more scientific contributions from other sources besides journal and conference papers to provide a more nuanced understanding of GenAI applications for K-12 students and teachers in practice. Since this study focuses solely on how GenAI has been employed for teaching and learning, other papers focusing on GenAI applications, including perspectives of other education stakeholders (e.g., policymakers), should be considered. Collecting these details will provide holistic information about GenAI for K-12 education.

## 5 Conclusion

This research focuses on the actual experiences of teachers and students using GenAI within the K-12 context. Given the increasing accessibility of GenAI in schools, it is crucial to understand how to use GenAI responsibly and effectively to enhance learning. Despite significant concerns about authorship, authenticity, and ethical implications that dominate discussions on GenAI use in education, the tool is here to stay. Consequently, there have been attempts to develop guidance for using GenAI across different subject domains (e.g., ), which involve gathering views and experiences from various education stakeholders. Beyond sharing opinions about the implications of these powerful AI tools, evidence of how GenAI has been applied in practice, within classrooms or intervention studies conducted with teachers and students, will serve as concrete guidelines for its use in the K-12 context.

As the future of K-12 education will feature personalized learning journeys, inclusivity, and empowered educators (), efforts must be directed toward creating frameworks and building resources to realize the full potential of GenAI in shaping the educational landscape. Current findings indicate that most research on GenAI use focuses on higher education populations and adult learners, with empirical exploration centered on perspectives, conceptions, and experiences rather than actual implementation of AI tools. Some perspective-gathering papers provide short training or workshops on GenAI use (for education leaders, in-service, or pre-service teachers) before collecting their views. Future reviews should synthesize these findings and detail the training elements. This study also observed a lack of research on students and teachers with special needs or learning disabilities, highlighting the need for research on GenAI and inclusive education in the K-12 context. Additionally, literature has not explored differences in GenAI tool use across various contexts, such as the rural–urban dichotomy, and how practices differ between students and teachers in these settings. As revealed in the study, gaps exist in the context of ECE, special needs education, and rural context in relation to GenAI use which are important areas that should be considered for future research agendas. Finally, although the papers explored how GenAI has assisted in writing and English, there is still much to learn about how GenAI supports language teaching and learning, particularly within the K-12 system.

## **Webpage Content** 
Title: Top AI Case Studies in Education 2025

URL Source: https://www.raisesummit.com/post/ai-case-studies-education

Markdown Content:
[Back to All News ![Image 1](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66f11b59c8366f8c2c21551f/690b2d440b13aea7748b8389_arrow%20icon.svg)](https://www.raisesummit.com/news)

![Image 2](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66f11b59c8366f8c2c215596/699d6fb73a0e958ff02451a0_698e6a71676cd2891cb336d8-1770947871926.avif)

### Top AI Case Studies in Education 2025

Published on

February 13, 2026

Real AI-in-education case studies: how generative AI boosted learning, cut IEP time, eased admin work, and revealed urgent training and ethics gaps.

In 2025, AI reshaped education worldwide, with **86% of institutions using generative AI**. Its role isn’t about replacing teachers but supporting them in areas like lesson planning, personalized learning, and reducing administrative tasks. Key insights include:

*   **AI adoption surged**: Use by students rose 26 percentage points, with 45% of educators still lacking training.
*   **Special education benefited**: AI reduced IEP preparation time by 90%, improving both efficiency and outcomes.
*   **Higher education embraced AI**: Universities like ASU and Louisiana used AI for administrative tasks, student growth, and literacy programs.
*   **Challenges remain**: Concerns about plagiarism and the training gap persist, highlighting the need for clearer guidelines.

AI’s presence in education is growing, but success depends on balancing human input with technological tools to improve learning experiences.

![Image 3: AI in Education 2025: Key Statistics and Adoption Trends](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66f11b59c8366f8c2c215596/699d6fb83a0e958ff024522f_698e6a71676cd2891cb336d8-1770947192593.jpg)

AI in Education 2025: Key Statistics and Adoption Trends

## Scaling AI in Education: A [Khanmigo](https://www.khanmigo.ai/) case study: Shawn Jansepar

![Image 4: Khanmigo](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66f11b59c8366f8c2c215596/699d6fb83a0e958ff0245202_2c54069d7b33efaa13e116e92194f391.jpeg)

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3E7VAZaTG9M)
## AI Implementation Case Studies in Education

Three institutions in the United States have shown how AI can reshape education when applied with clear goals and strong support systems.

**Lamont Elementary School District** adopted [Inkwire](https://inkwire.co/), an AI tool designed for competency-based project creation. This streamlined the process of designing projects and eased the workload for teachers, allowing them to focus more on teaching rather than planning.

The **University of Louisiana System** introduced a different initiative with its "Empowering AI Literacy for Students" programme, launched in spring 2025. This free, self-paced, 16-hour course - developed with state grant funding - has already reached 82,000 participants. The curriculum includes AI history, ethics, best practices, digital literacy, and data privacy. Upon completion, participants earn a digital badge to demonstrate their AI knowledge. Dr. Colleen Carraher Wolverton incorporated this microcredential into her "MGMT 455" course as extra credit. She noticed that students who were initially reluctant to use AI began applying it for practical purposes, such as drafting professional emails. Dr. Katie Dawson, Associate Vice President of Enrolment, Innovation, and Talent Strategy, highlighted the value of microcredentials:

> "Microcredentials are a powerful way to recognise and validate learning that complements a student's degree. They highlight in-demand skills, such as project management, data analytics, or AI literacy, giving students credentials that align with workforce needs" [[3]](https://louisiana.edu/distancelearning/news/preparing-students-ai-first-world-ul-system-launches-new-ai-microcredential).

Meanwhile, **[Arizona State University](https://www.asu.edu/) (ASU)** launched its AI Innovation Challenge in February 2024. Within just two weeks, the initiative attracted over 175 proposals, and by July 2024, more than 200 projects were underway across 80% of ASU’s academic units [[4]](https://www.govtech.com/education/higher-ed/complete-college-america-offers-case-studies-for-ai-in-higher-ed)[[5]](https://openai.com/index/asu). Winners received four-month ChatGPT Edu licences, with IT and instructional design teams providing support. One standout project was the "Sam" chatbot, developed in the College of Health Solutions. This tool allowed students to practise patient-provider interactions, offering realistic scenarios to build motivational skills and deliver qualitative feedback. Clinical Professor Colleen Cordes praised its effectiveness, while ASU Chief Information Officer Lev Gonick shared a key insight:

> "What we've learned at ASU is that if you want to focus on the impact of technology, start by asking the community what they want to solve for" [[5]](https://openai.com/index/asu).

Together, these examples highlight the importance of clear objectives and strong institutional support in making AI a meaningful part of the educational experience. The next section will explore the trends and lessons that have emerged from these initiatives.

## AI in Special Education: Reducing Administrative Work

Special education teachers face a daunting administrative workload. During the 2022–23 school year, **7.5 million students in the United States** - 15% of public school enrollment - required Individualized Education Programs (IEPs) [[6]](https://www.govtech.com/education/k-12/ai-for-ieps-new-tools-could-mean-less-paperwork-better-plans). These documents can stretch up to 50 pages, and with **70% of public schools reporting special education teacher vacancies** in 2023–24, the pressure on remaining staff has become immense [[6]](https://www.govtech.com/education/k-12/ai-for-ieps-new-tools-could-mean-less-paperwork-better-plans).

AI platforms are stepping in to ease this burden by automating "procedural compliance" - the extensive documentation that consumes hours of educators' time. In July 2025, Sanford-based company Better Speech introduced **[Streamline](https://www.streamline-sped.com/)**, an AI-powered platform for managing special education. The results? IEP preparation time dropped by **90%**, shrinking from 3 hours to just 10 minutes. Speech-language pathology (SLP) teams also reported improved therapy efficiency and better outcomes for students [[7]](https://www.eschoolnews.com/newsline/2025/07/01/first-ai-powered-special-education-management-platform-helps-districts-reach100-iep-compliance). CEO Ranan Lachman explained the mission behind this innovation:

> "Our goal isn't just to save time - it's to give educators and therapy providers their purpose back" [[7]](https://www.eschoolnews.com/newsline/2025/07/01/first-ai-powered-special-education-management-platform-helps-districts-reach100-iep-compliance).

AI isn't just cutting time; it's improving the quality of IEPs. A study involving preschool educators revealed that teachers using AI to draft IEP goals scored between **9.1 and 10 on a 10-point quality scale**, compared to a range of **5.5 to 9.2** for those working without AI [[6]](https://www.govtech.com/education/k-12/ai-for-ieps-new-tools-could-mean-less-paperwork-better-plans). Adoption of such technology is growing rapidly. By the 2024–25 school year, **57% of special education teachers** were using AI to assist with IEPs or 504 plans, up from 39% the year before [[8]](https://www.edweek.org/teaching-learning/teachers-are-using-ai-to-help-write-ieps-advocates-have-concerns/2025/10). Beyond paperwork, AI tools are also delivering actionable insights.

For example, in early 2026, Rose Prust, a Special Education Teacher at Lopez Island School District, used AI tools like **[Magic School](https://www.magicschool.ai/)** and **[Ablespace](https://www.ablespace.io/)** to refine IEP goals for students with complex needs. By analyzing interaction data through Ablespace, the AI discovered that a student with cortical visual impairment responded better to auditory cues than visual ones. This insight led to a shift towards multi-sensory instruction in the student's IEP, resulting in improved cause-and-effect comprehension within just one week [[9]](https://www.citygov.com/article/ai-meets-iep-reimagining-special-education-with-smart-tools).

Andrea Harkins-Brown, Program Director at Johns Hopkins University, highlighted the broader potential:

> "If AI can help me with the procedural compliance, which is the nuts and bolts, then team members hypothetically have more time for what we call substantive compliance, which is making sure the document is a true reflection of what the child needs" [[6]](https://www.govtech.com/education/k-12/ai-for-ieps-new-tools-could-mean-less-paperwork-better-plans).

This shift from administrative tasks to personalized support is transforming how educators allocate their time. AI's growing role in special education is enabling teachers to move beyond paperwork, focusing instead on delivering meaningful, tailored instruction to their students.

## Key Trends and Lessons from 2025 AI Case Studies

The education landscape in 2025 shows what’s possible when institutions use AI with purpose and strategy. It’s no longer just about adopting new tools - real success is seen in areas like student retention, administrative efficiency, and tailored support.

One standout trend is the use of predictive analytics for early intervention. For example, [Ivy Tech Community College](https://www.ivytech.edu/) in Indiana implemented an AI system to flag at-risk students within the first two weeks of the semester. The results were impressive: 98% of the students who received targeted interventions boosted their grades to at least a C, preventing 3,000 students from failing altogether[[10]](https://digitaldefynd.com/IQ/ai-in-schools-case-studies). This highlights how proactive measures, guided by AI, are changing outcomes for students.

Another clear advantage of AI is its ability to ease administrative burdens. At Georgia Institute of Technology, "Jill Watson", an AI-powered teaching assistant built on IBM’s Watson, managed most routine student questions in large-scale online courses. This drastically cut response times and allowed human teaching assistants to focus on more complex issues[[10]](https://digitaldefynd.com/IQ/ai-in-schools-case-studies). Similarly, Singapore’s Ministry of Education introduced automated tools to mark English assignments, assessing grammar, spelling, and syntax. This freed up teachers to focus on fostering creativity and critical thinking in their students[[10]](https://digitaldefynd.com/IQ/ai-in-schools-case-studies). These examples show how AI can handle repetitive tasks efficiently, but they also underline a critical gap: the need for better training.

Despite these advancements, a lack of AI training for educators and students remains a pressing issue. Surveys reveal that 45% of educators and 52% of students have not received any AI training, even as institutional leaders advocate for AI adoption[[1]](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/education/blog/2025/08/ai-in-education-report-insights-to-support-teaching-and-learning). Pat Yongpradit, Chief Academic Officer of [Code.org](https://code.org/) and Lead of [TeachAI](https://www.teachai.org/), highlighted the importance of addressing this gap:

> "Teachers are saying, 'I need training, it needs to be high quality, relevant, and job-embedded…' In reality, people require guidance and that means teachers and administrators going through professional development."[[1]](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/education/blog/2025/08/ai-in-education-report-insights-to-support-teaching-and-learning)

The lesson here is clear: successful AI integration isn’t just about acquiring the right tools. It requires thoughtful implementation, clear policies, ongoing professional development, and a "human-in-the-loop" approach. By keeping educators at the heart of the process, AI can scale its benefits - handling routine tasks while enhancing personalised learning experiences.

## [RAISE Summit](https://www.raisesummit.com/): Learning from AI in Education Case Studies

![Image 5: RAISE Summit](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66f11b59c8366f8c2c215596/699d6fa422202692be48bb00_b9809a81140ec8366f15221ded661aab.jpeg)

As the role of AI in education continues to grow, the **RAISE Summit** stands out as a key event for professionals eager to explore its potential. This annual gathering at the Carrousel du Louvre in Paris draws over 7,000 attendees, 2,000 companies, and more than 280 speakers, offering a unique opportunity for educators to dive into real-world AI applications. The summit provides not just theoretical insights but also practical tools and case studies to help institutions successfully integrate AI into their frameworks.

What sets RAISE Summit apart is its hands-on approach. Sessions focused on education include live demonstrations of tools like Socratic tutoring systems, with institutions such as [MIT RAISE](https://raise.mit.edu/) leading the way. These interactive showcases allow attendees to experience AI-powered teaching methods firsthand, bridging the gap between understanding the concept and applying it effectively.

**Networking opportunities** are another cornerstone of the summit. With participants from over 80 countries, educators can connect with peers to tackle common challenges in AI adoption. Discussions often revolve around overcoming infrastructure limitations, such as low bandwidth or reliance on feature phones in resource-constrained settings. The summit also emphasizes culturally responsive AI solutions, ensuring that technology aligns with diverse educational needs. As Cynthia Breazeal, Director of MIT RAISE, aptly stated:

> "Whether you're a learner, a parent, a policymaker, AI and education now go hand in hand." [[2]](https://raise.mit.edu/news/ai-in-the-hands-of-learners-highlights-from-the-2025-mit-ai-and-education-summit)

Panel discussions at the summit delve into critical questions about pedagogy and AI. For instance, sessions like "AI for Creative Learning" explore which traditional teaching practices should evolve to meet the demands of a changing society. Professor Mitch Resnick highlights a key concern:

> "Because AI could add some incremental advantages to what I see as outmoded approaches to pedagogy, it could reinforce them, re-entrench them, and not allow for the type of changes that we need for a changing society." [[2]](https://raise.mit.edu/news/ai-in-the-hands-of-learners-highlights-from-the-2025-mit-ai-and-education-summit)

These discussions aim to ensure that AI is used to innovate education rather than simply modernize outdated methods.

For those ready to take actionable steps, the summit offers flexible ticket options. The PRO pass (€999) grants full access to sessions, workshops, and networking events, while the VIP pass (€1,899) includes premium experiences and deeper industry connections. Emerging developers and startups can opt for a more affordable validated pass at €599, making the event accessible to a wide range of participants, regardless of their stage in AI adoption.

## Conclusion: The Future of AI in Education

By 2025, AI has evolved from a supplementary tool to a central component of modern education, reshaping learning experiences while maintaining the indispensable role of educators.

These case studies highlight the need for AI integration that respects local contexts and prioritizes human-centered approaches. Success stories often share a focus on design that considers diverse needs and cultural nuances. Stefania Giannini, Assistant Director-General for Education at [UNESCO](https://www.unesco.org/en), captures this sentiment perfectly:

> "The future of education will be shaped by the policy choices that we make about education investment, about pedagogy, about governance and about the ethical principles we uphold" [[12]](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/unesco-convenes-global-leaders-digital-learning-week-2025-shape-inclusive-human-centred-futures-ai).

This shift is steering education away from one-size-fits-all, English-dominated models toward systems that embrace linguistic and contextual diversity. Projects like Rwanda's WhatsApp-based RAISE initiative and [France Éducation International](https://www.france-education-international.fr/)'s multilingual Cybèle chatbot are excellent examples of this localized approach. The numbers speak volumes: 86% of educational organizations now use generative AI, and 76% of global leaders consider AI literacy a fundamental skill for basic education [[1]](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/education/blog/2025/08/ai-in-education-report-insights-to-support-teaching-and-learning).

However, there’s still a pressing need to close the training gap. Collaborative platforms and professional development opportunities are vital to ensuring AI serves as a creative ally rather than a source of stress or confusion for educators.

The future focus must move beyond simply adopting AI to fully embedding it in ways that enhance creativity and critical thinking. Initiatives like the [Day of AI](https://dayofai.org/curriculum-resources) curriculum, which reached over 2 million students across 175 countries in 2025 [[11]](https://raise.mit.edu/stories/2025-day-of-ai-impact-report), illustrate how AI fluency is becoming a foundational skill for the next generation. As Ana Lucía Pérez, a 10th-grade student from Puerto Rico, wisely points out:

> "Change doesn't start with perfection. It starts with curiosity and courage" [[2]](https://raise.mit.edu/news/ai-in-the-hands-of-learners-highlights-from-the-2025-mit-ai-and-education-summit).

For educators, this means embracing lifelong learning and innovative strategies to unlock AI’s full potential. Thoughtful integration and consistent professional growth will remain key to ensuring AI drives meaningful progress in education.

## FAQs

### How do schools train teachers for AI fast?

Schools are adopting focused, efficient approaches to help teachers get up to speed with AI. These include **online training programs** aimed at improving AI understanding, **industry-sponsored hubs** designed to quickly develop specific skills, and **pilot projects** where educators test AI tools directly in their classrooms. Additionally, **professional development sessions** are offered to ensure teachers can effectively use these tools in real-world teaching scenarios. The emphasis is on providing practical, easy-to-access training, so educators can seamlessly incorporate AI into their teaching methods.

### How can AI cut admin work without risking student data?

AI tools are transforming administrative tasks in education by making them more efficient while prioritizing student data protection. For instance, secure, FERPA-compliant solutions utilize advanced **Data Loss Prevention (DLP)** technology to redact and safeguard sensitive information. These tools handle tasks like grading and scheduling, freeing up valuable time for educators and staff.

To maintain both security and efficiency, these systems integrate features like **encryption**, **access controls**, and **audit trails**. This ensures that compliance with privacy regulations is upheld without sacrificing productivity.

### How do institutions prevent AI plagiarism and misuse?

Institutions are tackling the challenges of AI plagiarism and misuse by combining detection tools, clear policies, and education initiatives. AI detection tools are used to spot machine-generated content, though their accuracy can sometimes be inconsistent. To address this, many institutions place emphasis on educating students about the ethical use of AI and creating assessments that make misuse less tempting. By focusing on these strategies, they aim to encourage transparency, responsible behaviour, and academic integrity, rather than relying solely on punitive actions.

To begin, I want to provide a little bit of the context that Gemini’s deep research revealed. The first point here is probably not surprising, but it’s a good starting point of reference. Anyone connected with schools has most likely noticed how fast generative AI has been adopted by both students and staff. The adoption rate has been so fast that it has outpaced schools’ abilities to keep up with these changes. The human is at both ends of the equation—the beginning and the end.

The most effective strategies reimagined and improved the learning experience at the student level. So with that context in mind, let me share some lists with you. I created them by combining points from both Gemini and ChatGPT deep research results. The first list is a summary of the three most popular teacher uses of generative AI.

**Transition Music with Rena’s Children 3:50**Here are your three, here are your three tips. Here are your three tips.

**Paul Beckermann 3:55**So number one: differentiation and scaffolding. This is not only popular, but also effective as it improves accessibility and comprehension for diverse learners. This use was prominently highlighted by both ChatGPT and Gemini.

Number two: resource generation. This is related to number one, but it’s broader and includes streamlining administrative tasks such as generating IEPs, lesson plans, and content outlines. These tasks can be done with generative AI chat bots like ChatGPT and Gemini, and they can also be facilitated with teacher-specific tools like Magic School and School AI.

And number three: assessment generation. Teachers have been frequently using AI to help create test questions, align quizzes, and put together diagnostic reports.

**Paul Beckermann 4:26**This not only streamlines the time-consuming process of grading, but it also provides insights to guide data-driven instruction when used to create formative assessments. It also provides valuable practice opportunities for students. AI can create self-grading quizzes, flashcards, study guides, and more to provide immediate feedback that can be both valuable and timely.

So those are the most common ways teachers are using generative AI. Now let me shift to student uses. While teacher-centric practices are important and can free up valuable time for teachers to do more work individually with students, the student-facing strategies are the ones that have the most potential for transforming the actual learning experiences. Number one: AI-powered tutors.

**Paul Beckermann 5:08**This was a top strategy on both lists, and it makes sense. Tutoring is one of the most impactful approaches we can implement in the classroom. ChatGPT cites the Edutopia article, “AI tutors can work with the right guardrails.” These AI tutors mimic the benefits of one-on-one instruction, adjusting to student needs, providing hints step-by-step, and prompting deeper thinking. Studies cited in the article point out that students using the guided AI tutor scored dramatically higher on practice problems without harming performance on real tests. Teachers also report higher engagement and motivation when students use these tutors to explore material at their own pace.

**Paul Beckermann 6:18**Number two: differentiated learning materials. This one ties directly back to one of the teacher time-saving strategies, and it’s definitely a win-win item on the list. Not only does AI help save time and make differentiation more possible, it also has a positive impact on student learning, removing barriers by improving student access to the content at appropriate levels.

Number three: automated feedback. Feedback is key to the learning process. Students need to know if they’re on the right track or not so they can make the necessary changes to improve. Feedback is also one of the most time-consuming tasks a teacher faces each day. Tools like Magic School and School AI have developed student-facing AI tools in their ecosystems that provide automated feedback to students on their work, often shaped by teacher input during the design phase of the process. Enlighten…

**Paul Beckermann 6:58**…AI is a newer product that is gaining popularity as a writing feedback and assessment tool, one that isn’t intended to replace the teacher, but rather help to make timely feedback on writing more efficient and realistic.

Number four: interactive role-playing via AI chat bots. In some ways, this is like the automated feedback in the form of a character or historical figure. Teachers are leveraging prompts to direct chat bots to take on personas and carry on conversations with students. Tools like Khanmigo and Magic School have pre-made templates that teachers can share with students and require very little work on the teacher’s part. Engaging with these personas is both engaging and insightful. For instance, students can now speak with Thomas Jefferson about the Declaration of Independence, or chat with Atticus Finch, the lawyer in _To Kill a Mockingbird_.

**Paul Beckermann 7:48**World Language teachers can even use this as a way for their students to have conversations with the chat bot in a language that they’re studying. It’s great practice. While these experiences may occasionally communicate incorrect content, they can provide a safe and feedback-rich learning opportunity for students.

Number five: project-based learning. Rather than ban AI, many teachers are redesigning assignments to incorporate generative AI as a tool, in some ways “AI-proofing” their assignments and assessments. The key is to target authentic learning opportunities and then help students define and understand the steps in that process where AI both fits and is acceptable. Project-based learning is an opportunity to push deeper learning and problem-solving in a real-world, authentic context. The AI acts as a knowledgeable problem-solving partner in the process. To foster transparency, some teachers will have students document when and how they use their AI partner during the process.

**Paul Beckermann 8:43**Tasks that are often targeted include drafting, generating, and revising content in repeated cycles with the student as the active creator.

Number six: AI-assisted writing and revision. This one is a bit controversial and an area that has caused concern among some teachers, especially writing teachers. How do we make sure that students are still learning to write on their own, while also empowering them with the skills and knowledge about how AI might help in the process? There is no perfect answer to this question, and many adults are still trying to figure out how to use it in their own writing. In many cases, teachers are working to help students identify which tasks in the writing process are AI-friendly and which should be done without the use of generative AI. A big part of that involves open and honest communication. It also means providing examples and guidance, such as how to use AI to spark ideas and suggest improvements.

**Paul Beckermann 9:43**Sample prompts can be shared with students to help in this process.

And number seven: AI literacy and ethics exercises. Teachers have realized that they need to help students learn how to navigate and use generative AI, both for the sake of academic integrity and to help students become knowledgeable, skilled users of generative AI, both in and out of the classroom. Students need to know how AI works, its limitations, and how to use it effectively and responsibly. Tools like AI Trust You from the Laguna Beach Unified School District and free resources from organizations like News Literacy Project and Common Sense Media are available to help guide teachers through this process.

All right, that’s a lot, and I admit each of these items on the list probably warrants its own podcast episode. Still, I think a general overview is helpful. It’s a way to reflect on your own use of generative AI and potentially set some new goals for yourself.

**Paul Beckermann 10:48**Which strategies from the list have you tried, and which are areas that you could still explore? Are there any areas of generative AI use that you haven’t tried that might potentially save you time and improve student learning? If the answer is yes, pick one, dig in and give it a try.

To learn more about today’s topic and explore other free resources, visit Avid Open Access.org. Specifically, I encourage you to check out the article collection, “AI in the K-12 classroom,” and, of course, be sure to join Rena Winston and me every Wednesday for our full-length podcast _Unpacking Education_, where we’re joined by exceptional guests and explore education topics that are important to you. Thanks for listening. Take care and thanks for all you do. You make a difference.

## **Webpage Content** 
Title: 5 Proven Practices to Integrate AI into K-12 Education

URL Source: https://www.hanoverresearch.com/insights-blog/k-12-education/developing-k-12-ai-literacy-for-your-district

Published Time: 2026-01-29T20:33:42+00:00

Markdown Content:
## Artificial intelligence technology in schools is here to stay. Learn how to thoughtfully integrate AI into K-12 education with five practical tips.

Generative artificial intelligence, often simply called AI, has carved out a permanent place within schools. While AI tools have great potential to enhance teaching, learning, and operations, unmanaged use introduces significant risks. [84% of K-12 students](https://www.hanoverresearch.com/reports-and-briefs/k-12-education/ai-best-practices-in-k-12-education/) now use AI technology, yet K-12 AI integration remains fragmented, with many schools and districts lacking clear policies or guidance that keeps pace with AI’s widespread use.

Without [a systemwide AI integration plan](https://www.hanoverresearch.com/k-12-ai-framework/), K-12 organizations risk facing learning disruptions, data security concerns, and being left behind in an evolving technological landscape. To prepare staff and students for the future, it’s critical for K-12 leadership to prioritize developing a comprehensive strategy for appropriately integrating AI into their districts and schools.

Drawn from real-world examples shared by experts during Hanover’s webinar, [Navigating AI in Schools: Policies, Pitfalls, and Possibilities](https://www.hanoverresearch.com/webinars/k-12-education/navigating-ai-in-schools-policies-pitfalls-and-possibilities/), the following five proven practices will help set your K-12 organization on the path to successful AI integration.

### 1. Start with a Clear Vision and Flexible AI Policy

A successful AI strategy begins with a shared vision that feels grounded in your community’s values, while still preparing staff and students for a rapidly changing future. K-12 organizations that co-create this vision with staff, students, families, and other community members build trust and increase buy-in from the start.

A strong, future-ready AI vision should articulate how AI will enhance, not replace, human connection in schools. Consider how AI can be used to strategically advance organizational goals such as personalized learning, operational efficiency, or improved data practices.

Your AI policy should translate that vision into a living, adaptable framework that outlines:

*   Responsible use, ethics, and academic integrity expectations
*   Data privacy and security requirements
*   Guardrails that set boundaries for AI tools
*   Permissions and limitations around when, where, and how AI tools may be used

Because AI tools evolve quickly, your policy should be designed for easy updates as new capabilities emerge, risks or compliance needs shift, or community expectations change. A clear vision paired with flexible policy gives staff and students confidence, helping them navigate AI safely and intentionally.

##### _Build a comprehensive AI integration strategy with Hanover’s K-12 AI framework. [Learn more.](https://www.hanoverresearch.com/k-12-ai-framework/)_

### 2. Identify and Fill Operational Gaps for Improved Efficiency

Many of AI’s benefits extend far beyond the classroom. When used strategically, AI can reduce administrative burden, accelerate routine tasks, and free staff to focus more time on student-centered work within schools.

Begin with a targeted needs assessment to pinpoint gaps where AI could improve operational efficiency. K-12 organizations seeing success with AI integration consistently emphasize that human oversight when using AI for any task is non‑negotiable. AI can draft, recommend, and summarize, but staff must verify the accuracy of outputs and make final decisions.

[Westport Public Schools](https://www.hanoverresearch.com/testimonial/k-12-education/westport-public-schools-improves-survey-quality-and-data-analysis-with-hanover/), a district that champions successful AI use, has streamlined its operations with tools such as:

*   **Virtual Board of Education agent**: A custom AI bot built by uploading years of board meeting videos that helps staff anticipate board questions, test ideas, and refine materials before meetings.
*   **Communication agent**: Automates first drafts of press releases, analyzes social media sentiment, and helps leaders stay connected to community perceptions and concerns.
*   **Policy agent**:A bot trained on district policy manuals and state statutes that quickly locates relevant requirements and can draft emails or documents aligned to official policy.

When K-12 organizations close operational gaps with AI, they reclaim valuable time, increase consistency, and enhance the quality of decision-making across the system. These operational improvements also lay the foundation for [broader AI adoption](https://www.hanoverresearch.com/k-12-ai-framework/), creating early wins that show staff how AI can reduce burdens rather than add to them.

### 3. Drive Educator AI Adoption Through Strategic Professional Learning

Educator adoption is essential because staff are the primary translators of any new tool into daily practice across classrooms. While many educators already use AI, levels of confidence and effectiveness still vary widely, especially when moving from basic use to high-impact applications.

Start by benchmarking AI literacy and conducting a needs assessment to understand how staff are using AI and where they need support. Surveys, focus groups, or conversations during staff meetings can surface what’s already working and where staff want clearer guidance. Use these insights to design professional learning that is aligned with educator needs and AI literacy levels.

To build momentum:

*   **Model and reinforce from the top**: Leaders should build confidence in AI by regularly demonstrating practical use that’s tied back to the organization’s vision and guardrails.
*   **Anchor professional development in real workflows**: Prioritize training and guidance for classroom and operational tasks and provide low-stakes time to test out tools with support.
*   **Scale through peer examples**: Make time during staff meetings to spotlight what’s working, share prompts and processes, and normalize questions and iteration.

This needs-based professional learning approach accelerates the shift from experimentation to consistent practice, strengthening educators’ confidence in instructional and operational use and positioning AI as a tool that empowers their work rather than threatens it.

### 4. Elevate Student AI Literacy Beyond Basic Functions

Although most students are familiar with AI, many use AI tools only as a simple search engine or text generator. To truly prepare them for college, careers, and responsible digital citizenship, K-12 organizations must help students move beyond surface‑level use.

Start by clearly defining what AI readiness means for your organization. When crafting your definition, take workforce and college expectations into consideration. Then, embed AI literacy within existing curriculum rather than creating a standalone course. This keeps learning relevant and applicable to real academic tasks.

Key strategies include:

*   Teaching students to treat AI as a thought partner, not a replacement for their own thinking
*   Addressing ethical and responsible use, including the risks of academic dishonesty, the need to fact-check claims and verify sources, and understanding data privacy and digital footprints
*   Encouraging use of AI to examine assumptions and explore alternative perspectives
*   Designing separate grade‑, program‑, and subject‑specific guidelines for AI use

These approaches help students use AI to enhance learning, maintain academic integrity, and build skills that transfer into higher education and the workforce. This deeper level of AI literacy empowers students to become thoughtful problem solvers, ensuring they are ready to use AI responsibly and strategically.

##### _Leverage AI technology to enhance learning and operations with insights from our 2026 Trends in K-12 Education report. [Get the report.](https://www.hanoverresearch.com/reports-and-briefs/k-12-education/2026-trends-in-k-12-education/)_

### 5. Apply Proven Change Management Principles

While AI feels revolutionary, its integration relies on the same change management practices that have always worked when introducing new technologies in education.

Begin by assessing where your organization is now with AI adoption and where you want to be. Then, map the steps needed to bridge that gap. Throughout the process, ensure the focus is on supporting your organization’s larger mission and strategic goals through meaningful AI integration.

When K-12 organizations approach AI with the same intentionality used for other major shifts, such as the introduction of Multi‑Tiered Systems of Support frameworks or standards-aligned curriculum adoption efforts, they reduce uncertainty. This reinforces the idea that AI is not a disruptive, unwelcome addition, but instead a thoughtful enhancement to existing organizational priorities.

### Moving Toward Strategic, Systemwide K-12 AI Integration

Despite widespread AI usage in K-12 education, [only 33](https://www.aiforeducation.io/ai-resources/state-ai-guidance)U.S. states and Puerto Rico have issued any official AI guidance for schools to date. It’s evident that ignoring or banning AI in schools has the potential to worsen its risks, rather than mitigate them. Without direction, students and staff turn to AI tools independently, without guardrails to ensure safe and responsible use.

K-12 leaders now have a critical opportunity to shape how their communities navigate this technology. Each organization’s path will look different, but the foundational practices outlined here will help you build a responsible, effective [AI integration strategy](https://www.hanoverresearch.com/k-12-ai-framework/) that thoughtfully prepares your staff and students for the future.

You've probably heard colleagues talking about AI tools that generate lesson plans in minutes. Maybe you've seen the headlines about how AI will "transform education." And maybe you're thinking: _I barely have time to eat lunch, let alone become a prompt engineer._

Here's what you actually need to know: AI curriculum generators can [save teachers significant time](https://www.waltonfamilyfoundation.org/the-ai-dividend-new-survey-shows-ai-is-helping-teachers-reclaim-valuable-time) each week, time you can redirect to what matters most, like connecting with students. But they're not magic, and they're definitely not here to replace your expertise. These tools work best when teachers maintain control, review outputs for accuracy, and make final decisions about what reaches the classroom.

## What are AI curriculum generators?

AI curriculum generators are software tools that use artificial intelligence to create educational materials like lesson plans, worksheets, assessments, and differentiated content. Unlike general-purpose chatbots, these tools are built specifically for educators and come pre-loaded with educational frameworks, learning objectives, and grade-level standards.

When you input parameters like subject area, grade level, learning objectives, and student needs, an AI curriculum generator produces draft materials you can review, modify, and use in your classroom. Think of it as having a first draft ready in minutes instead of starting from a blank page every time you need to create something new.

## What AI curriculum generators actually do for teachers

Think of AI curriculum generators as specialized tools built specifically for K-12 classrooms, not generic chatbots.

Unlike asking generic AI chatbots to "write me a lesson plan," [purpose-built education AI tools](https://schoolai.com/blog/ai-lesson-planning-guide-teachers) come with Common Core and state standards already integrated. They're designed with FERPA and COPPA compliance built in, which matters when you're working with student data. And they generate classroom-ready materials, not generic content you'd need to completely rebuild.

## How AI curriculum tools cut planning time without losing control

A significant concern teachers express about AI: "It just doesn't work well." And sometimes that's true. According to domain-specific research on lesson planning, educators note that "the more you are versed in understanding AI and generating AI output, the more you're able to recognize" its limitations.

When teachers use AI curriculum generators to create differentiated texts, they don't just hit "generate" and walk away. They review the materials first. Educators implementing these tools note that AI-generated questions sometimes have multiple correct answers, so keeping a close eye on what's produced is essential.

That's actually how these tools are meant to work. You're using AI the same way you'd use a teaching assistant: delegating routine tasks while keeping final decisions in your hands. As [AI integration research](https://schoolai.com/blog/ai-lesson-planning-guide-teachers) emphasizes, successful AI implementation helps teachers focus on "building relationships and a sense of classroom community."

Here's what this could look like in practice: A sixth-grade teacher [uses AI to create](https://schoolai.com/blog/ai-lesson-plan-generator-standards-aligned) three versions of the same science text: one at grade level, one simplified for struggling readers, and one translated into Spanish for ELL students. She reviews each version for accuracy. Total time: 15 minutes instead of two hours.

## How AI curriculum generators make differentiation possible

You know the differentiation dilemma: You're supposed to reach advanced students, struggling students, and everyone in between, all at the same time, with limited planning periods. According to [research from Gallup-Walton](https://www.waltonfamilyfoundation.org/the-ai-dividend-new-survey-shows-ai-is-helping-teachers-reclaim-valuable-time), educators and parents see promise in AI tools for tasks like saving time and supporting personalized learning.

But most AI tools aren't developed with ELLs in mind, so your knowledge of your students' needs is essential for reviewing what gets generated.

## What to look for in student-safe AI curriculum tools

Not all AI tools are created equal, and this matters more in K-12 than anywhere else. When evaluating tools, focus on these essential criteria:

*   **FERPA and COPPA documentation:** Federal protections require K-12 schools to ensure vendors handle student data appropriately through contracts and documented privacy practices.

*   **Built-in standards alignment:** Look for tools with Common Core and state standards integrated, not just generic content generation.

*   **Clear data practices:** Specifically ask how data is stored, who can access it, how long it's retained, and whether data is used for algorithm training.

## How SchoolAI helps teachers control AI curriculum generation

SchoolAI is designed specifically to address what teachers need: tools that save time without requiring you to become an AI expert.

With SchoolAI, you can create interactive learning experiences customized for any lesson, subject, or grade level. The platform includes standards-guided content creation tools that provide Common Core standards alignment. You can either build lessons from scratch or adapt existing templates, with built-in teacher dashboards to track how students use the platform safely.

You can layer these together to create comprehensive, differentiated learning experiences.

Because SchoolAI is built for K-12, it includes [FERPA and COPPA compliance](https://schoolai.com/trust) with teacher dashboards providing visibility and control over every student interaction.

## Start using an AI curriculum generator on Monday

You don't need to revolutionize your entire practice overnight. Pick one specific, repetitive task: creating differentiated reading materials, generating varied practice problems, or drafting parent updates. Try using an [AI curriculum generator](https://schoolai.com/blog/ai-lesson-plan-generator-standards-aligned) for that task, review what gets generated, adjust it, and use it with students.

Artificial intelligence is no longer a peripheral tool in education. It is woven into how students study, how teachers plan lessons, and how institutions make decisions. In 2026, the conversation has shifted from whether to use AI to how to use it well.

These statistics come from primary research from 2025 and 2026 by Microsoft, McKinsey, Pew Research Center, and other credible institutions. They reveal what's actually happening in classrooms, corporate training programs, and online learning platforms right now.

Whether you are an educator, an administrator, or a policymaker, these figures offer a grounded picture of where AI in education stands right now.

Feel free to jump to the topic you're most interested in:

*   [Statistics on student and teacher AI adoption](https://www.engageli.com/blog/ai-in-education-statistics#adoption)
*   [Statistics on AI education market growth and adoption](https://www.engageli.com/blog/ai-in-education-statistics#growth)
*   [Statistics on AI's impact on learning outcomes](https://www.engageli.com/blog/ai-in-education-statistics#outcomes)
*   [Statistics on AI in corporate training](https://www.engageli.com/blog/ai-in-education-statistics#corporate)
*   [Statistics on personalized learning benefits](https://www.engageli.com/blog/ai-in-education-statistics#personalized)
*   [Statistics on the future of AI in education](https://www.engageli.com/blog/ai-in-education-statistics#future)

[](https://www.engageli.com/blog/ai-in-education-statistics)
## AI adoption and usage statistics

### 1. 85% of teachers and 86% of students used AI during the 2024-25 school year.

AI adoption in K-12 education has reached near-universal levels among both educators and students. In the United States, student use of AI for school-related purposes jumped 26% since last school year, while educator use rose 21% over the same period. This rapid, simultaneous adoption across both groups signals a fundamental shift in how teaching and learning happen day to day. The most common applications include research and content gathering (44%), creating lesson plans (38%), summarizing information (38%), and generating classroom materials (37%). [1, 2]

### 2. Teachers who use AI tools at least weekly save an average of 5.9 hours per week, the equivalent of six full weeks per school year.

This finding, from the Gallup-Walton Family Foundation survey of more than 1,000 teachers, represents a meaningful reduction in the administrative burden that has long contributed to teacher burnout and attrition. The most common time-saving applications include lesson planning, grading support, generating classroom materials, and drafting communications to parents. When teachers get hours back in their week, they can redirect that time toward direct student interaction and the relational work that no AI can replace.[3]

### 3. 92% of higher education students now use generative AI in some form, up from 66% in 2024.

The Higher Education Policy Institute's annual survey of UK students found that AI use surged more in a single year than in all prior years combined. Nearly 9 in 10 students (88%) acknowledged using generative AI tools for tests in 2025. This pace of adoption has outrun most institutional policy frameworks, creating a significant governance gap that universities are now racing to close.[4, 5]

### 4. 69% of teachers say AI tools have improved their teaching methods and skills.

A 2025 EdWeek survey found that beyond saving time, AI is actively improving how teachers teach. 59% of teachers said AI had enabled more personalized instruction, and high school teachers are the most active adopters, with 69% reporting generative AI use, compared with 42% of elementary teachers and just 33% of pre-K teachers. This gradient reflects the greater availability of AI tools designed for secondary and post-secondary content.[6, 7]

![Image 1: Downloadable how-to guides, research, and white papers designed for better online learning](https://www.engageli.com/hs-fs/hubfs/Downloadable%20how-to%20guides%2c%20research%2c%20and%20white%20papers%20designed%20for%20better%20online%20learning%20(3).png?width=750&height=422&name=Downloadable%20how-to%20guides%2c%20research%2c%20and%20white%20papers%20designed%20for%20better%20online%20learning%20(3).png)

[](https://www.engageli.com/blog/ai-in-education-statistics)
## Market growth and adoption statistics

### 5. The global AI in education market was valued at $7.05 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $136.79 billion by 2035.

The global AI in education market was valued at approximately $7.05 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $136.79 billion by 2035, growing at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of roughly 35%.To put that trajectory in perspective, the broader global learning and development market already exceeds $350 billion, and AI is increasingly the engine driving its expansion.

In July 2025, Microsoft announced an investment of more than $4 billion specifically in AI education initiatives, targeting schools, community colleges, and nonprofits through its newly launched Microsoft Elevate Academy. That commitment underscores how seriously major technology companies now view education as a strategic AI deployment frontier.[8, 9]

### 6. 86% of education organizations now use generative AI, which is the highest adoption rate of any industry.

While education has historically lagged behind other sectors in technology adoption, AI implementation has been remarkably swift. Educational institutions can deploy AI tools quickly to address immediate challenges like creating quiz questions, generating lesson plans, and providing feedback. The high adoption rate, documented in IDC research cited in Microsoft's 2025 AI in Education Report, demonstrates that AI tools are meeting real needs in educational practice. [1]

### 7. The Asia-Pacific region shows the fastest AI education market growth at 48% compound annual growth rate.

The region's explosive growth stems from large, rapidly expanding populations with growing educational needs and cultural attitudes that highly value educational achievement. Many Asia-Pacific countries are investing heavily in educational technology as part of broader economic development strategies, creating substantial demand for scalable, effective AI solutions. [10]

### 8. Only 20% of universities have a formal AI policy in place, even as 56% of students and educators believe their institution is unprepared to manage AI.

A February 2026 Coursera survey of more than 4,200 students and educators across five countries found that AI adoption has dramatically outpaced governance. At the K-12 level, the gap is just as wide: as of December 2024, only 31% of U.S. public schools had a written AI policy, according to U.S. Department of Education data. Institutions that close this gap first will be better positioned to capture the benefits of AI while managing its risks. [5, 11]

[](https://www.engageli.com/blog/ai-in-education-statistics)
## Learning outcomes and effectiveness statistics

### 9. 80% of students globally say AI has positively supported their learning experience.

The Coursera AI in Higher Education Report, released in February 2026, found that four in five students report AI has improved their academic performance. 70% believe AI will improve exam performance and the overall quality of higher education, and 63% say they use AI for less than half of their academic tasks, suggesting most students are using it as a supplement rather than a replacement for their own thinking.[5]

### 10. Students using an AI tutor scored significantly higher than those in traditional classes, according to a randomized controlled trial.

A peer-reviewed randomized controlled trial published in _Scientific Reports_ in June 2025 found that an AI tutor outperformed traditional in-class learning, with an effect size between 0.73 and 1.3 standard deviations. Students using the AI tutor not only achieved substantially higher post-test scores than their peers in traditional active learning environments, but did so in less time. The AI group’s median time on task was 49 minutes, compared with 60 minutes for in-class learners. This represents one of the strongest experimental results to date on the effectiveness of AI tutoring. [5]

### 11. Students in AI-enhanced active learning programs achieve 54% higher test scores than those in traditional environments.

The improvement spans multiple subjects (mathematics, science, language arts, and social studies) and appears on standardized assessments designed independently of AI-enhanced learning. AI systems excel at identifying and addressing knowledge gaps before they compound into larger problems, ensuring students have solid foundations before advancing to more complex concepts. [13]

### 12. AI-powered active learning generates 10 times more engagement than traditional passive learning methods.

AI enables interactive experiences regardless of class size or format, transforming passive lecture-based learning into participatory experiences. Students in AI-enhanced environments participate more in discussions, ask more questions, and spend additional time with course materials outside class. The technology facilitates real-time adjustments based on student engagement levels. [13]

### 13. AI-powered assessment tools provide feedback that is 10 times faster than traditional methods.

Immediate feedback allows students to correct misconceptions while material remains fresh in their minds, significantly improving learning effectiveness. AI enables continuous micro-assessments rather than periodic major tests, providing more accurate pictures of student understanding and enabling timely interventions when students need additional support. [14]

### 14. 95% of college faculty believe generative AI will increase students' overreliance on these tools, and 90% say it will diminish critical thinking skills.

A January 2026 national survey by the American Association of Colleges and Universities found that faculty concerns about AI are running high. 73% of faculty reported having personally handled academic integrity issues related to student AI use, and 83% predicted AI will decrease students' attention spans. These concerns are not a reason to avoid AI, but they are a clear signal that intentional pedagogical design matters enormously. [15]

[](https://www.engageli.com/blog/ai-in-education-statistics)
## AI in corporate training statistics

### 15. Businesses collectively spend $400 billion on training annually, yet 74% of companies report they are not keeping up with their organization's demand for new skills.

Research from the Josh Bersin Company, published in February 2026, found that despite massive investment in learning and development, most organizations are falling behind. AI is now reshaping this market from the ground up, enabling personalized, adaptive training at a scale and speed that traditional content libraries and instructor-led programs cannot match. [16]

### 16. AI-powered corporate training leads to a 57% increase in learning efficiency.

Employees complete training programs faster while demonstrating superior mastery and better retention when tested weeks or months later. Most importantly, they apply new skills more effectively in actual work situations. AI optimizes learning experiences by focusing on areas where each person needs development rather than covering material they already know. [9]

### 17. 66% of education and business leaders say they would not hire someone without AI literacy skills.

Microsoft's 2025 AI in Education Report found that AI fluency has become a baseline hiring requirement across industries. Upskilling employees in AI is now the top workforce strategy for 47% of leaders over the next 12 to 18 months. 54% of global educators and 76% of global education leaders view AI literacy as an essential component of basic education for every student. [1]

### 18. 77% of global workers express willingness to retrain or learn new AI-related skills.

Workers recognize that AI tools make jobs more efficient and effective, leading to increased productivity and job satisfaction. They understand that AI literacy is becoming a competitive advantage, with employers increasingly seeking candidates who can work effectively with AI systems. This willingness represents a significant shift from historical resistance to technological change. [17]
