[](https://www.engageli.com/blog/ai-in-education-statistics)
## Personalized learning through AI statistics

### 19. AI-powered personalized learning increases student engagement rates by up to 60% and learning efficiency by 57%.

When AI tailors learning paths to individual students, the results compound across multiple dimensions simultaneously: engagement rises, time-to-mastery falls, and retention improves. 74% of adult learners report greater motivation in AI-enhanced courses due to personalized experiences, and 67% of students agree that AI helps them study faster or more efficiently. [9]

### 20. 75% of students feel more motivated in personalized AI learning environments compared to 30% in traditional classrooms.

Personalized learning experiences tailored to individual interests, learning styles, and knowledge levels help students feel more competent and confident. Students gain greater autonomy over their educational experiences, exploring topics that interest them and progressing at their own pace rather than following rigid, predetermined paths. [14]

### 21. Schools implementing AI-powered personalized learning observed a 12% increase in student attendance and a 15% reduction in dropout rates.

AI-powered early warning systems analyze multiple data points such as declining grades, reduced participation, irregular attendance, and changes in engagement to identify at-risk students before they disengage entirely. Early identification enables educators to provide targeted support, and when educational content aligns with individual interests and learning styles, students find school more relevant and worthwhile. [14]

### 22. Students achieve 70% better course completion rates with AI-personalized learning compared to traditional approaches.

AI bridges differences in learning styles, cultural backgrounds, and prior educational experiences, which is particularly valuable in global educational contexts with diverse student populations. AI-powered collaboration tools also help overcome language barriers and communication challenges that can impede international learning programs. [18]

[](https://www.engageli.com/blog/ai-in-education-statistics)
## Future trends for AI in education statistics

### 23. The OECD's Digital Education Outlook 2026 warns that performing a task with AI does not automatically lead to learning.

The OECD's landmark 2026 report on digital education found that students with access to general-purpose AI chatbots produced higher-quality outputs than peers, but this advantage disappeared and sometimes reversed in exams when access was removed. Educational AI tools designed with intentional pedagogical purpose, by contrast, showed sustained improvements. The report argues that learning to work with AI, and to know when not to, is now a foundational skill alongside reading and mathematics. [19]

### 24. Students in low-income and rural areas are the least likely to report that their schools allow or integrate AI use.

A Gallup survey cited by NPR in August 2025 found that the AI opportunity is not being distributed equally. Globally, 24.7% of the working-age population in the Global North now uses generative AI tools, compared with only 14.1% in the Global South. UNESCO's 2025 survey of higher education institutions found that around 70% of institutions in Europe and North America have or are developing AI guidance, compared with just 45% in Latin America and the Caribbean. Closing this equity gap is as important as any other challenge in AI education policy. [20, 21, 22]

### 25. Workers using AI tools could add $7.9 trillion to the global economy, but only if AI literacy scales across the entire workforce.

The economic impact comes from productivity improvements as workers learn to leverage AI tools effectively in their specific roles. Education and training play crucial roles in realizing this potential: widespread AI literacy is necessary for the productivity gains to scale. 92% of business leaders expect to boost AI spending over the next three years, reflecting a broad consensus that the investment in AI-enabled learning is not optional. [23]

Engageli is redefining active learning through AI-powered tools that make engagement, collaboration, and personalized instruction not only possible, but scalable.

**Real-time engagement insights and dynamic interventions**

Instructors using Engageli gain access to detailed, real-time engagement data that tracks speaking time, attendance trends, chat activity, and sentiment across the class, small groups, and individuals. AI-powered recommendations guide instructors to take timely action, whether that’s launching a quick poll, reshuffling groups, or pausing for clarification. This allows for immediate, evidence-based instructional decisions that keep learners on track.

What once took hours of production can now be done in a fraction of the time without compromising on quality or engagement.

Engageli’s AI tutors provide learners with personalized feedback and review based on their performance and the specific content of each class. Students can ask questions, revisit key moments in recorded sessions, and receive tailored support, making learning more efficient and outcomes more equitable. In asynchronous lessons, students can ask questions and role play in a safe and controlled environment.

**AI-driven course summaries and accessibility tools**

After each [live or recorded session](https://www.engageli.com/products-services/virtual-classroom), Engageli auto-generates class summaries that can be emailed to attendees. Students can also generate an in-the-moment summary of the previous five minutes of the session in their student notebooks. These tools make content more accessible, reinforce learning, and keep all learners aligned, whether they attended live or on-demand.

**Proven impact**

Data from Engageli’s own [active learning impact study](https://www.engageli.com/active-learning-impact-study) shows that when learners are engaged in active, AI-enhanced environments, outcomes improve significantly:

*   16x more nonverbal engagement
*   54% higher test scores compared to passive learning settings

These results mirror broader market trends. AI in education is no longer optional: it’s infrastructure. With Engageli, organizations gain not just tools but a proven strategy to drive retention, proficiency, and ROI through scalable active learning.

Interested in learning more about Engageli's AI-powered solutions? [Take a tour](https://www.engageli.com/product-tour) of our products or [book a personalized demo](https://www.engageli.com/start/getting-started).

## AI in education FAQs

### What is AI in education?

AI in education refers to artificial intelligence technologies that enhance teaching, learning, and administrative processes. This includes personalized learning systems that adapt to individual student needs, automated grading and feedback tools, intelligent tutoring systems, and predictive analytics that help identify at-risk students. AI also assists teachers with content creation, lesson planning, and administrative tasks.

### How effective is AI compared to traditional teaching methods?

Research demonstrates significant advantages for AI-enhanced education. Students in AI-powered learning environments achieve 54% higher test scores, show 30% better learning outcomes, and experience 10x more engagement compared to traditional methods. A 2025 randomized controlled trial published in Scientific Reports found AI tutoring outperformed in-class active learning with an effect size between 0.73 and 1.3 standard deviations. AI also improves completion rates by 70% and reduces dropout rates by 15% while simultaneously increasing student motivation.

### What are the main benefits of AI in education?

Key benefits of AI in education include personalized learning experiences that adapt to individual needs, immediate feedback that accelerates learning, improved student engagement and motivation, better learning outcomes and test scores, significant time savings for teachers (nearly six weeks per year for weekly AI users), early identification of at-risk students, and more efficient corporate training programs (57% increase in learning efficiency).

### How can educational institutions implement AI effectively?

Successful AI implementation in educational institutions involves starting with specific use cases like automated grading or content creation, ensuring proper teacher training and support, maintaining focus on pedagogical goals, protecting student privacy and data security, and measuring outcomes to demonstrate value. The OECD's 2026 Digital Education Outlook recommends moving beyond general-purpose AI tools toward purpose-built educational AI that is designed to produce durable learning gains, not just better task outputs. Platforms like Engageli provide comprehensive solutions that integrate multiple AI capabilities.

### What does the future hold for AI in education?

The AI education market is projected to grow from $7.05 billion in 2025 to $136.79 billion by 2035. Key trends include increased personalization, more sophisticated assessment tools, better integration with existing educational systems, expanded use in corporate training, and AI-powered collaboration tools for global learning experiences. 92% of business leaders plan to increase AI spending, indicating continued rapid adoption. The most pressing challenge ahead is equity: ensuring that the benefits of AI in education reach students in low-income, rural, and under-resourced communities at the same rate as those in well-funded institutions.

## AI in education FAQs

### What is AI in education?

AI in education refers to artificial intelligence technologies that enhance teaching, learning, and administrative processes. This includes personalized learning systems that adapt to individual student needs, automated grading and feedback tools, intelligent tutoring systems, and predictive analytics that help identify at-risk students. AI also assists teachers with content creation, lesson planning, and administrative tasks.

### How effective is AI compared to traditional teaching methods?

Research demonstrates significant advantages for AI-enhanced education. Students in AI-powered learning environments achieve 54% higher test scores, show 30% better learning outcomes, and experience 10x more engagement compared to traditional methods. A 2025 randomized controlled trial published in Scientific Reports found AI tutoring outperformed in-class active learning with an effect size between 0.73 and 1.3 standard deviations. AI also improves completion rates by 70% and reduces dropout rates by 15% while simultaneously increasing student motivation.

### What are the main benefits of AI in education?

Key benefits of AI in education include personalized learning experiences that adapt to individual needs, immediate feedback that accelerates learning, improved student engagement and motivation, better learning outcomes and test scores, significant time savings for teachers (nearly six weeks per year for weekly AI users), early identification of at-risk students, and more efficient corporate training programs (57% increase in learning efficiency).

### How can educational institutions implement AI effectively?

Successful AI implementation in educational institutions involves starting with specific use cases like automated grading or content creation, ensuring proper teacher training and support, maintaining focus on pedagogical goals, protecting student privacy and data security, and measuring outcomes to demonstrate value. The OECD's 2026 Digital Education Outlook recommends moving beyond general-purpose AI tools toward purpose-built educational AI that is designed to produce durable learning gains, not just better task outputs. Platforms like Engageli provide comprehensive solutions that integrate multiple AI capabilities.

### What does the future hold for AI in education?

The AI education market is projected to grow from $7.05 billion in 2025 to $136.79 billion by 2035. Key trends include increased personalization, more sophisticated assessment tools, better integration with existing educational systems, expanded use in corporate training, and AI-powered collaboration tools for global learning experiences. 92% of business leaders plan to increase AI spending, indicating continued rapid adoption. The most pressing challenge ahead is equity: ensuring that the benefits of AI in education reach students in low-income, rural, and under-resourced communities at the same rate as those in well-funded institutions.

## AI adoption and usage statistics

### 1. 85% of teachers and 86% of students used AI during the 2024-25 school year.

AI adoption in K-12 education has reached near-universal levels among both educators and students. In the United States, student use of AI for school-related purposes jumped 26% since last school year, while educator use rose 21% over the same period. This rapid, simultaneous adoption across both groups signals a fundamental shift in how teaching and learning happen day to day. The most common applications include research and content gathering (44%), creating lesson plans (38%), summarizing information (38%), and generating classroom materials (37%). [1, 2]

### 2. Teachers who use AI tools at least weekly save an average of 5.9 hours per week, the equivalent of six full weeks per school year.

This finding, from the Gallup-Walton Family Foundation survey of more than 1,000 teachers, represents a meaningful reduction in the administrative burden that has long contributed to teacher burnout and attrition. The most common time-saving applications include lesson planning, grading support, generating classroom materials, and drafting communications to parents. When teachers get hours back in their week, they can redirect that time toward direct student interaction and the relational work that no AI can replace.[3]

### 3. 92% of higher education students now use generative AI in some form, up from 66% in 2024.

The Higher Education Policy Institute's annual survey of UK students found that AI use surged more in a single year than in all prior years combined. Nearly 9 in 10 students (88%) acknowledged using generative AI tools for tests in 2025. This pace of adoption has outrun most institutional policy frameworks, creating a significant governance gap that universities are now racing to close.[4, 5]

### 4. 69% of teachers say AI tools have improved their teaching methods and skills.

A 2025 EdWeek survey found that beyond saving time, AI is actively improving how teachers teach. 59% of teachers said AI had enabled more personalized instruction, and high school teachers are the most active adopters, with 69% reporting generative AI use, compared with 42% of elementary teachers and just 33% of pre-K teachers. This gradient reflects the greater availability of AI tools designed for secondary and post-secondary content.[6, 7]

## AI in education FAQs

### What is AI in education?

AI in education refers to artificial intelligence technologies that enhance teaching, learning, and administrative processes. This includes personalized learning systems that adapt to individual student needs, automated grading and feedback tools, intelligent tutoring systems, and predictive analytics that help identify at-risk students. AI also assists teachers with content creation, lesson planning, and administrative tasks.

### How effective is AI compared to traditional teaching methods?

Research demonstrates significant advantages for AI-enhanced education. Students in AI-powered learning environments achieve 54% higher test scores, show 30% better learning outcomes, and experience 10x more engagement compared to traditional methods. A 2025 randomized controlled trial published in Scientific Reports found AI tutoring outperformed in-class active learning with an effect size between 0.73 and 1.3 standard deviations. AI also improves completion rates by 70% and reduces dropout rates by 15% while simultaneously increasing student motivation.

### What are the main benefits of AI in education?

Key benefits of AI in education include personalized learning experiences that adapt to individual needs, immediate feedback that accelerates learning, improved student engagement and motivation, better learning outcomes and test scores, significant time savings for teachers (nearly six weeks per year for weekly AI users), early identification of at-risk students, and more efficient corporate training programs (57% increase in learning efficiency).

### How can educational institutions implement AI effectively?

Successful AI implementation in educational institutions involves starting with specific use cases like automated grading or content creation, ensuring proper teacher training and support, maintaining focus on pedagogical goals, protecting student privacy and data security, and measuring outcomes to demonstrate value. The OECD's 2026 Digital Education Outlook recommends moving beyond general-purpose AI tools toward purpose-built educational AI that is designed to produce durable learning gains, not just better task outputs. Platforms like Engageli provide comprehensive solutions that integrate multiple AI capabilities.

The AI education market is projected to grow from $7.05 billion in 2025 to $136.79 billion by 2035. Key trends include increased personalization, more sophisticated assessment tools, better integration with existing educational systems, expanded use in corporate training, and AI-powered collaboration tools for global learning experiences. 92% of business leaders plan to increase AI spending, indicating continued rapid adoption. ## AI adoption and usage statistics

### 1. 85% of teachers and 86% of students used AI during the 2024-25 school year.

AI adoption in K-12 education has reached near-universal levels among both educators and students. In the United States, student use of AI for school-related purposes jumped 26% since last school year, while educator use rose 21% over the same period. This rapid, simultaneous adoption across both groups signals a fundamental shift in how teaching and learning happen day to day. The most common applications include research and content gathering (44%), creating lesson plans (38%), summarizing information (38%), and generating classroom materials (37%). [1, 2]

### 2. Teachers who use AI tools at least weekly save an average of 5.9 hours per week, the equivalent of six full weeks per school year.

This finding, from the Gallup-Walton Family Foundation survey of more than 1,000 teachers, represents a meaningful reduction in the administrative burden that has long contributed to teacher burnout and attrition. The most common time-saving applications include lesson planning, grading support, generating classroom materials, and drafting communications to parents. When teachers get hours back in their week, they can redirect that time toward direct student interaction and the relational work that no AI can replace.[3]

### 3. 92% of higher education students now use generative AI in some form, up from 66% in 2024.

The Higher Education Policy Institute's annual survey of UK students found that AI use surged more in a single year than in all prior years combined. Nearly 9 in 10 students (88%) acknowledged using generative AI tools for tests in 2025. This pace of adoption has outrun most institutional policy frameworks, creating a significant governance gap that universities are now racing to close.[4, 5]

### 4. 69% of teachers say AI tools have improved their teaching methods and skills.

A 2025 EdWeek survey found that beyond saving time, AI is actively improving how teachers teach. 59% of teachers said AI had enabled more personalized instruction, and high school teachers are the most active adopters, with 69% reporting generative AI use, compared with 42% of elementary teachers and just 33% of pre-K teachers. This gradient reflects the greater availability of AI tools designed for secondary and post-secondary content.[6, 7]

While education has historically lagged behind other sectors in technology adoption, AI implementation has been remarkably swift. ## Learning outcomes and effectiveness statistics

### 9. 80% of students globally say AI has positively supported their learning experience.

The Coursera AI in Higher Education Report, released in February 2026, found that four in five students report AI has improved their academic performance. 70% believe AI will improve exam performance and the overall quality of higher education, and 63% say they use AI for less than half of their academic tasks, suggesting most students are using it as a supplement rather than a replacement for their own thinking.[5]

### 10. Students using an AI tutor scored significantly higher than those in traditional classes, according to a randomized controlled trial.

A peer-reviewed randomized controlled trial published in _Scientific Reports_ in June 2025 found that an AI tutor outperformed traditional in-class learning, with an effect size between 0.73 and 1.3 standard deviations. Students using the AI tutor not only achieved substantially higher post-test scores than their peers in traditional active learning environments, but did so in less time. The AI group’s median time on task was 49 minutes, compared with 60 minutes for in-class learners. This represents one of the strongest experimental results to date on the effectiveness of AI tutoring. [5]

### 11. Students in AI-enhanced active learning programs achieve 54% higher test scores than those in traditional environments.

The improvement spans multiple subjects (mathematics, science, language arts, and social studies) and appears on standardized assessments designed independently of AI-enhanced learning. AI systems excel at identifying and addressing knowledge gaps before they compound into larger problems, ensuring students have solid foundations before advancing to more complex concepts. [13]

### 12. AI-powered active learning generates 10 times more engagement than traditional passive learning methods.

AI enables interactive experiences regardless of class size or format, transforming passive lecture-based learning into participatory experiences. Students in AI-enhanced environments participate more in discussions, ask more questions, and spend additional time with course materials outside class. The technology facilitates real-time adjustments based on student engagement levels. [13]

### 13. AI-powered assessment tools provide feedback that is 10 times faster than traditional methods.

Immediate feedback allows students to correct misconceptions while material remains fresh in their minds, significantly improving learning effectiveness. AI enables continuous micro-assessments rather than periodic major tests, providing more accurate pictures of student understanding and enabling timely interventions when students need additional support. [14]

### 14. 95% of college faculty believe generative AI will increase students' overreliance on these tools, and 90% say it will diminish critical thinking skills.

A January 2026 national survey by the American Association of Colleges and Universities found that faculty concerns about AI are running high. 73% of faculty reported having personally handled academic integrity issues related to student AI use, and 83% predicted AI will decrease students' attention spans. These concerns are not a reason to avoid AI, but they are a clear signal that intentional pedagogical design matters enormously. [15]

Workers recognize that AI tools make jobs more efficient and effective, leading to increased productivity and job satisfaction. They understand that AI literacy is becoming a competitive advantage, with employers increasingly seeking candidates who can work effectively with AI systems. This willingness represents a significant shift from historical resistance to technological change. [17]

## Personalized learning through AI statistics

### 19. AI-powered personalized learning increases student engagement rates by up to 60% and learning efficiency by 57%.

When AI tailors learning paths to individual students, the results compound across multiple dimensions simultaneously: engagement rises, time-to-mastery falls, and retention improves. 74% of adult learners report greater motivation in AI-enhanced courses due to personalized experiences, and 67% of students agree that AI helps them study faster or more efficiently. [9]

### 20. 75% of students feel more motivated in personalized AI learning environments compared to 30% in traditional classrooms.

Personalized learning experiences tailored to individual interests, learning styles, and knowledge levels help students feel more competent and confident. Students gain greater autonomy over their educational experiences, exploring topics that interest them and progressing at their own pace rather than following rigid, predetermined paths. [14]

### 21. Schools implementing AI-powered personalized learning observed a 12% increase in student attendance and a 15% reduction in dropout rates.

AI-powered early warning systems analyze multiple data points such as declining grades, reduced participation, irregular attendance, and changes in engagement to identify at-risk students before they disengage entirely. Early identification enables educators to provide targeted support, and when educational content aligns with individual interests and learning styles, students find school more relevant and worthwhile. [14]

### 22. Students achieve 70% better course completion rates with AI-personalized learning compared to traditional approaches.

AI bridges differences in learning styles, cultural backgrounds, and prior educational experiences, which is particularly valuable in global educational contexts with diverse student populations. AI-powered collaboration tools also help overcome language barriers and communication challenges that can impede international learning programs. [18]

## Future trends for AI in education statistics

### 23. The OECD's Digital Education Outlook 2026 warns that performing a task with AI does not automatically lead to learning.

The OECD's landmark 2026 report on digital education found that students with access to general-purpose AI chatbots produced higher-quality outputs than peers, but this advantage disappeared and sometimes reversed in exams when access was removed. Educational AI tools designed with intentional pedagogical purpose, by contrast, showed sustained improvements. The report argues that learning to work with AI, and to know when not to, is now a foundational skill alongside reading and mathematics. [19]

### 24. Students in low-income and rural areas are the least likely to report that their schools allow or integrate AI use.

A Gallup survey cited by NPR in August 2025 found that the AI opportunity is not being distributed equally. Globally, 24.7% of the working-age population in the Global North now uses generative AI tools, compared with only 14.1% in the Global South. UNESCO's 2025 survey of higher education institutions found that around 70% of institutions in Europe and North America have or are developing AI guidance, compared with just 45% in Latin America and the Caribbean. Closing this equity gap is as important as any other challenge in AI education policy. [20, 21, 22]

### 25. Workers using AI tools could add $7.9 trillion to the global economy, but only if AI literacy scales across the entire workforce.

The economic impact comes from productivity improvements as workers learn to leverage AI tools effectively in their specific roles. Education and training play crucial roles in realizing this potential: widespread AI literacy is necessary for the productivity gains to scale. 92% of business leaders expect to boost AI spending over the next three years, reflecting a broad consensus that the investment in AI-enabled learning is not optional. ## Introduction

Generative AI (GenAI) is reshaping the educational landscape, beyond teaching and learning. Unlike earlier waves of [education technology](https://www.oecd.org/en/about/projects/smart-data-and-digital-technology-in-education--artifical-intelligence,-learning-analytics-and-beyond.html), much of GenAI is freely accessible and largely used beyond institutional control due to its intuitiveness and versatility. The [_OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026_](https://doi.org/10.1787/062a7394-en)analyses emerging research that suggests GenAI can support learning when guided by clear teaching principles. However, if designed or used without pedagogical guidance, outsourcing tasks to GenAI simply enhances performance with no real learning gains. The Outlook highlights the benefits of GenAI as a tutor, partner and assistant, and synthesises experts’ evidence and insights on the design criteria that make it work for education.

37%

of lower secondary teachers used AI for their job in 2024 (TALIS 2024)

57%

of lower secondary teachers agree that AI helps to write or improve lesson plans

72%

of lower secondary teachers believe AI can harm academic integrity by letting students pass off work as their own

## Successfully performing a task with GenAI does not automatically lead to learning

Emerging evidence suggests that while general-purpose GenAI tools can enhance students’ performance on tasks, they do not necessarily lead to learning gains. Offloading cognitive tasks to general-purpose chatbots creates risks of metacognitive laziness and disengagement that may deter skill acquisition in the long run. Several studies indicate that although students with access to general-purpose GenAI tools produce higher-quality outputs than their peers, this advantage disappears – and sometimes reverses – in exams when access is removed. In contrast, educational GenAI tools designed or used with an intentional pedagogical purpose tend to show sustained improvements in learning.

## Using GenAI with pedagogical intent can improve learning and foster skills like critical thinking, creativity and collaboration

GenAI can improve learning gains if used with a clear pedagogical purpose, or when teaching strategies are redesigned to adapt to its availability. For example, in collaborative learning scenarios aligned with learning science, GenAI tools can increase student knowledge or strengthen their argumentation skills. GenAI can also make traditional digital tools more engaging and efficient. For example, Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) powered by GenAI can transform rigidly scripted digital tutors into digital pedagogical agents capable of questioning, nudging and shifting strategies through natural, dialogue-based interactions.

## Educational GenAI can augment human teaching and tutoring while preserving teachers’ agency

Robust research evidence demonstrates that inexperienced tutors can enhance the quality of their tutoring and improve student learning outcomes by using educational GenAI tools. By integrating teacher expertise into the design process, GenAI tools can amplify teachers' capacity to teach, creating benefits that exceed what either teachers or AI can achieve independently. Co-designing GenAI tools with teachers and end users is one way to ensure they deliver educational value.

## GenAI can boost scientific research and help streamline institutional operations

GenAI is increasingly supporting scientific research, which could be transformative for education research. For example, since the launch of ChatGPT, an increasing share of researchers are turning to GenAI tools for feedback on their papers – and for all steps of the research process. School administrators too see their tasks transformed: GenAI can streamline system and school management by improving a wide range of backend workflows. It can support the design of standardised assessment items, review curricular alignments, and tag and classify educational resources. Well-tuned, it also permits 24/7 good study and career guidance.

## What can governments and other education stakeholders do?

### Foster human-centred teaching and learning with GenAI

Learning and teaching should primarily aim to develop valued human knowledge and skills such as independent thinking and foundational skills across subjects, without GenAI, with educational GenAI, and then with general-purpose GenAI. GenAI should be used selectively and purposefully for pedagogical reasons to enrich learning and not replace cognitive effort or weaken the human relationships at the heart of education.

### Invest in educational GenAI research and development

As general-purpose GenAI tools are not designed specifically for learning, education systems should incentivise the development of tools that aim to enhance teaching and learning. Investing in educational GenAI grounded in learning science, co-created with teachers and learners, and supported by rigorous research on their effectiveness can open new possibilities for educational improvement. Governments and education stakeholders should also co-operate to research beneficial uses of GenAI in education.

### Shape an enabling policy environment for trustworthy GenAI

Jurisdictions should ensure that policy and regulatory frameworks protect learners and support learning while enabling innovation. Combined with ongoing stakeholder dialogue, clear expectations on privacy, safety, bias testing, age-appropriateness, transparency and alignment with educational objectives can create an enabling environment for the trustworthy and meaningful use of GenAI in education.

### Support an effective GenAI infrastructure for all

Jurisdictions should ensure equitable digital infrastructure and support (devices, connectivity, digital resources and professional learning opportunities) so that all students and teachers can benefit from GenAI. Providing curriculum-aligned GenAI resources, alternative solutions where divides persist, and sustained professional learning, enables effective, inclusive and meaningful uses of GenAI in education.

## How is Generative AI impacting education?

OECD research findings suggest that Generative AI can support learning when guided by clear teaching principles. However, when designed or used without pedagogical support, outsourcing tasks to GenAI will only enhance student performance without leading to real learning gains. The OECD’s latest Digital Education Outlook presents emerging evidence on its impact in classrooms across the world.

## Introduction

Generative AI (GenAI) is reshaping the educational landscape, beyond teaching and learning. Unlike earlier waves of [education technology](https://www.oecd.org/en/about/projects/smart-data-and-digital-technology-in-education--artifical-intelligence,-learning-analytics-and-beyond.html), much of GenAI is freely accessible and largely used beyond institutional control due to its intuitiveness and versatility. The [_OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026_](https://doi.org/10.1787/062a7394-en)analyses emerging research that suggests GenAI can support learning when guided by clear teaching principles. However, if designed or used without pedagogical guidance, outsourcing tasks to GenAI simply enhances performance with no real learning gains. The Outlook highlights the benefits of GenAI as a tutor, partner and assistant, and synthesises experts’ evidence and insights on the design criteria that make it work for education.

37%

of lower secondary teachers used AI for their job in 2024 (TALIS 2024)

57%

of lower secondary teachers agree that AI helps to write or improve lesson plans

72%

of lower secondary teachers believe AI can harm academic integrity by letting students pass off work as their own

## Successfully performing a task with GenAI does not automatically lead to learning

Emerging evidence suggests that while general-purpose GenAI tools can enhance students’ performance on tasks, they do not necessarily lead to learning gains. Offloading cognitive tasks to general-purpose chatbots creates risks of metacognitive laziness and disengagement that may deter skill acquisition in the long run. Several studies indicate that although students with access to general-purpose GenAI tools produce higher-quality outputs than their peers, this advantage disappears – and sometimes reverses – in exams when access is removed. In contrast, educational GenAI tools designed or used with an intentional pedagogical purpose tend to show sustained improvements in learning.

## Using GenAI with pedagogical intent can improve learning and foster skills like critical thinking, creativity and collaboration

GenAI can improve learning gains if used with a clear pedagogical purpose, or when teaching strategies are redesigned to adapt to its availability. For example, in collaborative learning scenarios aligned with learning science, GenAI tools can increase student knowledge or strengthen their argumentation skills. GenAI can also make traditional digital tools more engaging and efficient. For example, Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) powered by GenAI can transform rigidly scripted digital tutors into digital pedagogical agents capable of questioning, nudging and shifting strategies through natural, dialogue-based interactions.

## Educational GenAI can augment human teaching and tutoring while preserving teachers’ agency

Robust research evidence demonstrates that inexperienced tutors can enhance the quality of their tutoring and improve student learning outcomes by using educational GenAI tools. By integrating teacher expertise into the design process, GenAI tools can amplify teachers' capacity to teach, creating benefits that exceed what either teachers or AI can achieve independently. Co-designing GenAI tools with teachers and end users is one way to ensure they deliver educational value.

## GenAI can boost scientific research and help streamline institutional operations

GenAI is increasingly supporting scientific research, which could be transformative for education research. For example, since the launch of ChatGPT, an increasing share of researchers are turning to GenAI tools for feedback on their papers – and for all steps of the research process. School administrators too see their tasks transformed: GenAI can streamline system and school management by improving a wide range of backend workflows. It can support the design of standardised assessment items, review curricular alignments, and tag and classify educational resources. Well-tuned, it also permits 24/7 good study and career guidance.

## What can governments and other education stakeholders do?

### Foster human-centred teaching and learning with GenAI

Learning and teaching should primarily aim to develop valued human knowledge and skills such as independent thinking and foundational skills across subjects, without GenAI, with educational GenAI, and then with general-purpose GenAI. GenAI should be used selectively and purposefully for pedagogical reasons to enrich learning and not replace cognitive effort or weaken the human relationships at the heart of education.

### Invest in educational GenAI research and development

As general-purpose GenAI tools are not designed specifically for learning, education systems should incentivise the development of tools that aim to enhance teaching and learning. Investing in educational GenAI grounded in learning science, co-created with teachers and learners, and supported by rigorous research on their effectiveness can open new possibilities for educational improvement. Governments and education stakeholders should also co-operate to research beneficial uses of GenAI in education.

### Shape an enabling policy environment for trustworthy GenAI

Jurisdictions should ensure that policy and regulatory frameworks protect learners and support learning while enabling innovation. Combined with ongoing stakeholder dialogue, clear expectations on privacy, safety, bias testing, age-appropriateness, transparency and alignment with educational objectives can create an enabling environment for the trustworthy and meaningful use of GenAI in education.

### Support an effective GenAI infrastructure for all

Jurisdictions should ensure equitable digital infrastructure and support (devices, connectivity, digital resources and professional learning opportunities) so that all students and teachers can benefit from GenAI. Providing curriculum-aligned GenAI resources, alternative solutions where divides persist, and sustained professional learning, enables effective, inclusive and meaningful uses of GenAI in education.

## How is Generative AI impacting education?

OECD research findings suggest that Generative AI can support learning when guided by clear teaching principles. However, when designed or used without pedagogical support, outsourcing tasks to GenAI will only enhance student performance without leading to real learning gains. The OECD’s latest Digital Education Outlook presents emerging evidence on its impact in classrooms across the world.

## Introduction

Generative AI (GenAI) is reshaping the educational landscape, beyond teaching and learning. Unlike earlier waves of [education technology](https://www.oecd.org/en/about/projects/smart-data-and-digital-technology-in-education--artifical-intelligence,-learning-analytics-and-beyond.html), much of GenAI is freely accessible and largely used beyond institutional control due to its intuitiveness and versatility. The [_OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026_](https://doi.org/10.1787/062a7394-en)analyses emerging research that suggests GenAI can support learning when guided by clear teaching principles. However, if designed or used without pedagogical guidance, outsourcing tasks to GenAI simply enhances performance with no real learning gains. The Outlook highlights the benefits of GenAI as a tutor, partner and assistant, and synthesises experts’ evidence and insights on the design criteria that make it work for education.

37%

of lower secondary teachers used AI for their job in 2024 (TALIS 2024)

57%

of lower secondary teachers agree that AI helps to write or improve lesson plans

72%

of lower secondary teachers believe AI can harm academic integrity by letting students pass off work as their own

## Successfully performing a task with GenAI does not automatically lead to learning

Emerging evidence suggests that while general-purpose GenAI tools can enhance students’ performance on tasks, they do not necessarily lead to learning gains. Offloading cognitive tasks to general-purpose chatbots creates risks of metacognitive laziness and disengagement that may deter skill acquisition in the long run. Several studies indicate that although students with access to general-purpose GenAI tools produce higher-quality outputs than their peers, this advantage disappears – and sometimes reverses – in exams when access is removed. In contrast, educational GenAI tools designed or used with an intentional pedagogical purpose tend to show sustained improvements in learning.

## Using GenAI with pedagogical intent can improve learning and foster skills like critical thinking, creativity and collaboration

GenAI can improve learning gains if used with a clear pedagogical purpose, or when teaching strategies are redesigned to adapt to its availability. For example, in collaborative learning scenarios aligned with learning science, GenAI tools can increase student knowledge or strengthen their argumentation skills. GenAI can also make traditional digital tools more engaging and efficient. For example, Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) powered by GenAI can transform rigidly scripted digital tutors into digital pedagogical agents capable of questioning, nudging and shifting strategies through natural, dialogue-based interactions.

## Educational GenAI can augment human teaching and tutoring while preserving teachers’ agency

Robust research evidence demonstrates that inexperienced tutors can enhance the quality of their tutoring and improve student learning outcomes by using educational GenAI tools. By integrating teacher expertise into the design process, GenAI tools can amplify teachers' capacity to teach, creating benefits that exceed what either teachers or AI can achieve independently. Co-designing GenAI tools with teachers and end users is one way to ensure they deliver educational value.

## GenAI can boost scientific research and help streamline institutional operations

GenAI is increasingly supporting scientific research, which could be transformative for education research. For example, since the launch of ChatGPT, an increasing share of researchers are turning to GenAI tools for feedback on their papers – and for all steps of the research process. School administrators too see their tasks transformed: GenAI can streamline system and school management by improving a wide range of backend workflows. It can support the design of standardised assessment items, review curricular alignments, and tag and classify educational resources. Well-tuned, it also permits 24/7 good study and career guidance.

## What can governments and other education stakeholders do?

### Foster human-centred teaching and learning with GenAI

Learning and teaching should primarily aim to develop valued human knowledge and skills such as independent thinking and foundational skills across subjects, without GenAI, with educational GenAI, and then with general-purpose GenAI. GenAI should be used selectively and purposefully for pedagogical reasons to enrich learning and not replace cognitive effort or weaken the human relationships at the heart of education.

### Invest in educational GenAI research and development

As general-purpose GenAI tools are not designed specifically for learning, education systems should incentivise the development of tools that aim to enhance teaching and learning. Investing in educational GenAI grounded in learning science, co-created with teachers and learners, and supported by rigorous research on their effectiveness can open new possibilities for educational improvement. Governments and education stakeholders should also co-operate to research beneficial uses of GenAI in education.

### Shape an enabling policy environment for trustworthy GenAI

Jurisdictions should ensure that policy and regulatory frameworks protect learners and support learning while enabling innovation. Combined with ongoing stakeholder dialogue, clear expectations on privacy, safety, bias testing, age-appropriateness, transparency and alignment with educational objectives can create an enabling environment for the trustworthy and meaningful use of GenAI in education.

### Support an effective GenAI infrastructure for all

Jurisdictions should ensure equitable digital infrastructure and support (devices, connectivity, digital resources and professional learning opportunities) so that all students and teachers can benefit from GenAI. Providing curriculum-aligned GenAI resources, alternative solutions where divides persist, and sustained professional learning, enables effective, inclusive and meaningful uses of GenAI in education.

## How is Generative AI impacting education?

OECD research findings suggest that Generative AI can support learning when guided by clear teaching principles. However, when designed or used without pedagogical support, outsourcing tasks to GenAI will only enhance student performance without leading to real learning gains. The OECD’s latest Digital Education Outlook presents emerging evidence on its impact in classrooms across the world.

## Introduction

Generative AI (GenAI) is reshaping the educational landscape, beyond teaching and learning. Unlike earlier waves of [education technology](https://www.oecd.org/en/about/projects/smart-data-and-digital-technology-in-education--artifical-intelligence,-learning-analytics-and-beyond.html), much of GenAI is freely accessible and largely used beyond institutional control due to its intuitiveness and versatility. The [_OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026_](https://doi.org/10.1787/062a7394-en)analyses emerging research that suggests GenAI can support learning when guided by clear teaching principles. However, if designed or used without pedagogical guidance, outsourcing tasks to GenAI simply enhances performance with no real learning gains. The Outlook highlights the benefits of GenAI as a tutor, partner and assistant, and synthesises experts’ evidence and insights on the design criteria that make it work for education.

37%

of lower secondary teachers used AI for their job in 2024 (TALIS 2024)

57%

of lower secondary teachers agree that AI helps to write or improve lesson plans

72%

of lower secondary teachers believe AI can harm academic integrity by letting students pass off work as their own

## Successfully performing a task with GenAI does not automatically lead to learning

Emerging evidence suggests that while general-purpose GenAI tools can enhance students’ performance on tasks, they do not necessarily lead to learning gains. Offloading cognitive tasks to general-purpose chatbots creates risks of metacognitive laziness and disengagement that may deter skill acquisition in the long run. Several studies indicate that although students with access to general-purpose GenAI tools produce higher-quality outputs than their peers, this advantage disappears – and sometimes reverses – in exams when access is removed. In contrast, educational GenAI tools designed or used with an intentional pedagogical purpose tend to show sustained improvements in learning.

## Using GenAI with pedagogical intent can improve learning and foster skills like critical thinking, creativity and collaboration

GenAI can improve learning gains if used with a clear pedagogical purpose, or when teaching strategies are redesigned to adapt to its availability. For example, in collaborative learning scenarios aligned with learning science, GenAI tools can increase student knowledge or strengthen their argumentation skills. GenAI can also make traditional digital tools more engaging and efficient. For example, Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) powered by GenAI can transform rigidly scripted digital tutors into digital pedagogical agents capable of questioning, nudging and shifting strategies through natural, dialogue-based interactions.

## Educational GenAI can augment human teaching and tutoring while preserving teachers’ agency

Robust research evidence demonstrates that inexperienced tutors can enhance the quality of their tutoring and improve student learning outcomes by using educational GenAI tools. By integrating teacher expertise into the design process, GenAI tools can amplify teachers' capacity to teach, creating benefits that exceed what either teachers or AI can achieve independently. Co-designing GenAI tools with teachers and end users is one way to ensure they deliver educational value.

## GenAI can boost scientific research and help streamline institutional operations

GenAI is increasingly supporting scientific research, which could be transformative for education research. For example, since the launch of ChatGPT, an increasing share of researchers are turning to GenAI tools for feedback on their papers – and for all steps of the research process. School administrators too see their tasks transformed: GenAI can streamline system and school management by improving a wide range of backend workflows. It can support the design of standardised assessment items, review curricular alignments, and tag and classify educational resources. Well-tuned, it also permits 24/7 good study and career guidance.

## What can governments and other education stakeholders do?

### Foster human-centred teaching and learning with GenAI

Learning and teaching should primarily aim to develop valued human knowledge and skills such as independent thinking and foundational skills across subjects, without GenAI, with educational GenAI, and then with general-purpose GenAI. GenAI should be used selectively and purposefully for pedagogical reasons to enrich learning and not replace cognitive effort or weaken the human relationships at the heart of education.

### Invest in educational GenAI research and development

As general-purpose GenAI tools are not designed specifically for learning, education systems should incentivise the development of tools that aim to enhance teaching and learning. Investing in educational GenAI grounded in learning science, co-created with teachers and learners, and supported by rigorous research on their effectiveness can open new possibilities for educational improvement. Governments and education stakeholders should also co-operate to research beneficial uses of GenAI in education.

### Shape an enabling policy environment for trustworthy GenAI

Jurisdictions should ensure that policy and regulatory frameworks protect learners and support learning while enabling innovation. Combined with ongoing stakeholder dialogue, clear expectations on privacy, safety, bias testing, age-appropriateness, transparency and alignment with educational objectives can create an enabling environment for the trustworthy and meaningful use of GenAI in education.

### Support an effective GenAI infrastructure for all

Jurisdictions should ensure equitable digital infrastructure and support (devices, connectivity, digital resources and professional learning opportunities) so that all students and teachers can benefit from GenAI. Providing curriculum-aligned GenAI resources, alternative solutions where divides persist, and sustained professional learning, enables effective, inclusive and meaningful uses of GenAI in education.

## How is Generative AI impacting education?

OECD research findings suggest that Generative AI can support learning when guided by clear teaching principles. However, when designed or used without pedagogical support, outsourcing tasks to GenAI will only enhance student performance without leading to real learning gains. The OECD’s latest Digital Education Outlook presents emerging evidence on its impact in classrooms across the world.

**Case Study: Lamont (pages 6-9)**

During the summer of 2024, Learner-Centered Collaborative facilitated a three-day Project-Based Learning (PBL) workshop for educators in Lamont who were interested in bringing their unique Learning Model and Portrait of a Learner to life in their classrooms.

Following an introduction to our PBL design elements, this group launched into a yearlong PBL Innovation Cohort where they could brainstorm project ideas, test them out in the classroom, share their results, iterate their designs, and test again. Their design toolbox included Inkwire, a PBL designer that could reference Learner-Centered Collaborative’s PBL design elements, Lamont’s Portrait of a Learner, and Lamont’s Learning Model. This supports educators in their design of projects to ensure they are aligned with district frameworks, strategies, and desired outcomes.

Kelly Williams, Director of Strategic Partnerships and leader of Lamont’s Learner-Centered Innovation Cohort, noted, "Some educators were already using ChatGPT for their project designs, but Inkwire gave them a shortcut. It already had all the district’s foundational documents embedded within the tool and didn’t require special knowledge like “prompt engineering” to receive high-quality output."

With Inkwire, educators can generate project ideas aligned to district-specific standards and learner-centered outcomes, then receive multi-week project plans broken out into daily schedules. That structure doesn’t just save time–it deepens teachers’ understanding of the district’s learner-centered philosophy and how to apply it in practice.

Midway through the cohort experience, 88 percent of participants said they were excited and curious about the role of AI in education, and over 70 percent were using AI tools, including Inkwire, weekly. This frequency of use has helped participants develop an understanding of how to work with AI to get the best results possible.

For instance, Inkwire’s output wasn’t to be taken as 100% complete. “I can look at it and say, okay, day one, yes, I want to do that activity. I’ll skip day two, and I can probably combine days three and four,” said a fifth-grade educator at Alicante Elementary School in Lamont.

She emphasized that her PBL expertise was still needed to assess the quality of Inkwire’s output, but it saved her hours of time upfront creating the initial project plan so she could focus on the finer details of her daily lesson plans.

An important distinction between an application like Inkwire and a Large Language Model (LLM) like ChatGPT is that Inkwire is a one-way experience. With Inkwire, users can choose AI-generated ideas from a dropdown list or provide custom responses based on a preset list of question prompts. Once all answers are added, Inkwire creates a project plan. Compare that to an LLM where users engage in an open conversation, going back and forth, searching for the right things to say that will improve the output.

Antonio Aguilera, a seventh-grade world history educator at Mountain View Middle School, likes to use Inkwire as a brainstorming tool when he’s stumped on what type of project he wants to design that specifically targets one of the competencies that aligns with the district’s Portrait of a Learner.

“With Inkwire, it's easy to just click the dropdown. It's more user-friendly if you're not that tech-savvy. It’s also nice because in ChatGPT, if you forget to directly reference the Lamont Portrait of a Learner in your chat, then your results might be too generic, whereas with Inkwire, that's a non-issue because it's already integrated.” This points to the value of a tool that is pre-trained with district frameworks and materials as references.

Both Lamont educators mentioned taking advantage of what each tool does best. During the 2024-25 academic year, Inkwire’s strength was designing competency-aligned project plans, whereas an LLM like ChatGPT was a better thought partner for lesson plan design.

After receiving her project plan from Inkwire, a fifth-grade educator inserted it into ChatGPT and asked questions like: “Can you suggest what you would put on each slide for this topic? Can you give me a list of women who are in STEM? Can you make sure this is for fifth-grade students?”

Shortly after the year wrapped up, Inkwire released a new feature that provides educators with individual lesson plans and suggests detailed activities. This is a great addition, but it doesn’t make the educators’ use of ChatGPT irrelevant. There continues to be great value in stacking different AI tools together and taking advantage of what each does best.

“Inkwire is like your coach. It’s prompting you with these questions that train you to internalize this learner-centered mindset. The more I’m internalizing those questions for myself, the more I start to see teaching and learning through those questions more broadly,” -Kelly Williams

This cohort experience gave educators a new way to see themselves as teachers and learners. Going into the summer and the 2025-26 academic year, educators are excited to continue the journey and are already planning what projects they might try next.

During the final Celebration of Learning in May 2025, Lamont’s Innovation Cohort participants talked about how they saw themselves as learners throughout the experience. Many agreed with the sentiment shared by one participant about readiness: “I wasn’t fully ready to try PBL or work with an AI tool. I didn’t have it all mapped out. I just gave myself permission to try and learn along the way.” That willingness to try without knowing how everything would play out translated to a new relationship with students where educators can say, “I’m learning alongside you. We’re in this together.”

**Case Study: Escondido (pages 10-13)**

Escondido Union School District (EUSD) had already done the hard and foundational work of building a Framework for the Future: A Portrait of a Learner was in place, a Learning Model was in use, and educators were beginning to test learner-centered strategies in classrooms.

With so much change already happening, introducing a new technology like AI felt like a stretch. However, for North Broadway Elementary Principal Cherry Moore, she could already see this technology wasn't going to wait for anyone. Students and classroom educators were already tinkering with it on their own, so it was imperative to create space for open dialogue and experimentation.

Rather than launching AI broadly, the school partnered with Learner-Centered Collaborative in spring 2025 and formed a Design Team of innovative educators who were excited to put AI to the test.

Their primary tool for experimentation was the Learning Experience Accelerator (LEA) App, developed using Playlab. This application is a learning experience thought partner trained using Learner-Centered Collaborative’s research-based Learning Model and classroom strategies as well as Escondido’s Learner Profile competencies. It helps educators integrate those competencies and strategies into their daily instruction aligned to desired outcomes.

When educators began playing with the tool, “They all were like, 'wow, I can see this unlocking our teachers,'" recalled César Morales, Partner Lead for Escondido Union School District.

The Learning Experience Accelerator seamlessly integrates the district's unique Portrait of a Learner competencies and Learning Model, state standards, and LCC's learner-centered strategies so that the output is consistently aligned with the district's implementation goals.

When using the tool, educators answer questions about their grade level and describe a unit, project, or lesson they are planning to teach. The app then connects their idea to specific Portrait of a Learner competencies and shares success criteria based on their grade band. It also provides concrete strategies for explicitly teaching the relevant skills, providing feedback to learners, and designing opportunities for learners to demonstrate and reflect on the skills throughout the unit or project.

Notably, while the EUSD Design Team of early adopters was experimenting with the app, every educator in the school was building a knowledge base around the district's Framework for the Future.

"We had done some work with the district's new Learning Model (developed in collaboration with Learner-Centered Collaborative), so we had this foundation," reflected Cherry. "Then we started asking teachers to create a learning experience based on what they understood about the Learning Model to see if what they designed could produce the Whole-Learner Outcomes expressed in our district's Portrait of a Learner." Cherry felt it was imperative to develop this foundational knowledge prior to introducing the LEA app so educators could confidently assess and iterate on the outputs.

Once the foundation was in place throughout the school and the Design Team felt confident about how to get the most out of Playlab, the bot was introduced at an all-staff meeting where 5th-grade educator Katie Taylor demonstrated how to use the tool to rework an existing lesson.

Her colleagues watched as she selected relevant learner outcomes from their Portrait, received suggestions aligned to their Learning Model, and adapted the ideas to meet her classroom needs. The live demo was catalytic. “The tool builds confidence and has educators saying 'oh my gosh, I know more than I thought I knew about our Portrait and Learning Model,'" César shared. "This tool just elevates those connections for teachers."

“I think by August, we will be in a place where teachers will take a fresh look at the plans they made, go in and identify what Whole-Learner Outcomes their plans will hit, and then explore how students might self-assess based on the Whole-Learner Outcomes they’re developing. I feel like that’s when our teachers are going to be more energized and ready to have more tools to help them do that work.” -Cherry Moore

As they head into the summer and plan for the 2025-26 academic year, the emphasis will be on seeing the Learning Experience Accelerator App as a way to enhance unit planning and build capacity for designing Learner Profile aligned learning experiences.

North Broadway’s story shows that scaling AI use isn’t about urgency—it’s about strategy. With a clear vision, phased rollout, peer modeling, and purposeful tools, the school created conditions where innovation could grow without top-down mandates, but rather with authentic buy-in from educators.

**Conclusion (page 14)**

The stories from Lamont and Escondido remind us that AI is not a shortcut or a substitute for educator expertise—it’s a tool. When integrated within a clear and shared vision like a Framework for the Future, AI helps educators navigate the complexity of learner-centered models and translate big ideas into meaningful day-to-day practice. Tools like Inkwire and Playlab don’t replace professional judgment; they elevate it.

Change in education is not just about adopting new models; it’s about building the capacity of educators to implement them effectively. AI-enabled tools provide educators with specific ideas for bringing the Portrait of a Learner competencies into their daily lessons, units, and projects while implementing learner-centered strategies. These tools not only enhance learning design but also foster continuous professional learning and collaboration.

As learner-centered education continues to evolve, AI has the potential to serve as a powerful companion on the journey, enabling educators to design learning experiences that are more authentic, personalized, and competency-based. We hope these stories inspire you to explore how AI can support your team and the learners you serve!

During the 2022–23 school year, **7.5 million students in the United States** - 15% of public school enrollment - required Individualized Education Programs (IEPs) [[6]](https://www.govtech.com/education/k-12/ai-for-ieps-new-tools-could-mean-less-paperwork-better-plans). These documents can stretch up to 50 pages, and with **70% of public schools reporting special education teacher vacancies** in 2023–24, the pressure on remaining staff has become immense [[6]](https://www.govtech.com/education/k-12/ai-for-ieps-new-tools-could-mean-less-paperwork-better-plans).

AI platforms are stepping in to ease this burden by automating 'procedural compliance' - the extensive documentation that consumes hours of educators' time. In July 2025, Sanford-based company Better Speech introduced **[Streamline](https://www.streamline-sped.com/)**, an AI-powered platform for managing special education. The results? IEP preparation time dropped by **90%**, shrinking from 3 hours to just 10 minutes. Speech-language pathology (SLP) teams also reported improved therapy efficiency and better outcomes for students [[7]](https://www.eschoolnews.com/newsline/2025/07/01/first-ai-powered-special-education-management-platform-helps-districts-reach100-iep-compliance).

For example, in early 2026, Rose Prust, a Special Education Teacher at Lopez Island School District, used AI tools like **[Magic School](https://www.magicschool.ai/)** and **[Ablespace](https://www.ablespace.io/)** to refine IEP goals for students with complex needs. By analyzing interaction data through Ablespace, the AI discovered that a student with cortical visual impairment responded better to auditory cues than visual ones. This insight led to a shift towards multi-sensory instruction in the student's IEP, resulting in improved cause-and-effect comprehension within just one week [[9]](https://www.citygov.com/article/ai-meets-iep-reimagining-special-education-with-smart-tools).

**Key Trends and Lessons from 2025 AI Case Studies**
Despite these advancements, a lack of AI training for educators and students remains a pressing issue. Surveys reveal that 45% of educators and 52% of students have not received any AI training, even as institutional leaders advocate for AI adoption[[1]](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/education/blog/2025/08/ai-in-education-report-insights-to-support-teaching-and-learning). Pat Yongpradit, Chief Academic Officer of [Code.org](https://code.org/) and Lead of [TeachAI](https://www.teachai.org/), highlighted the importance of addressing this gap: 'Teachers are saying, "I need training, it needs to be high quality, relevant, and job-embedded…" In reality, people require guidance and that means teachers and administrators going through professional development.'[[1]](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/education/blog/2025/08/ai-in-education-report-insights-to-support-teaching-and-learning)

The lesson here is clear: successful AI integration isn’t just about acquiring the right tools. It requires thoughtful implementation, clear policies, ongoing professional development, and a 'human-in-the-loop' approach. By keeping educators at the heart of the process, AI can scale its benefits - handling routine tasks while enhancing personalised learning experiences.

**Future Trends and Recommendations**
The future focus must move beyond simply adopting AI to fully embedding it in ways that enhance creativity and critical thinking. Initiatives like the [Day of AI](https://dayofai.org/curriculum-resources) curriculum, which reached over 2 million students across 175 countries in 2025 [[11]](https://raise.mit.edu/stories/2025-day-of-ai-impact-report), illustrate how AI fluency is becoming a foundational skill for the next generation. As Ana Lucía Pérez, a 10th-grade student from Puerto Rico, wisely points out: 'Change doesn't start with perfection. It starts with curiosity and courage' [[2]](https://raise.mit.edu/news/ai-in-the-hands-of-learners-highlights-from-the-2025-mit-ai-and-education-summit).

For educators, this means embracing lifelong learning and innovative strategies to unlock AI’s full potential. Thoughtful integration and consistent professional growth will remain key to ensuring AI drives meaningful progress in education.

Recommendations focus on clear policies, human-in-the-loop models, and embedding AI literacy through initiatives like Day of AI. Future trends highlight moving beyond tool adoption to deeper integration that enhances creativity and critical thinking, with localized, culturally responsive approaches.

AI curriculum generators help by creating multiple versions of materials you'd never have time to produce manually:

For English language learners, AI tools can simplify text while maintaining grade-level concepts, provide vocabulary support at different proficiency levels, and even [translate materials](https://schoolai.com/blog/ai-translation-tools-multilingual-classrooms). But most AI tools aren't developed with ELLs in mind, so your knowledge of your students' needs is essential for reviewing what gets generated.

**Implementation Methods:**
Teachers who start small build sustainable uses rather than trying to implement AI everywhere at once. The goal isn't to use AI because it's trendy. The goal is to reclaim time for what brought you to teaching: working directly with students.
