## **Webpage Content** 
Title: The use of generative artificial intelligence in K-12 education: An introduction to the special issue of the Journal of Educational Research

URL Source: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913

Markdown Content:
## Abstract

To open this special issue of The Journal of Educational Research, I have collected a range of research reports on teaching and learning with generative artificial intelligence (GAI). To guide readers in exploring the contents of this special issue, I have provided a summary of each of the included research reports. I have organized the articles by educational context to provide readers with additional context for the articles and enhance the potential for translating the research into practice. I open and conclude my introduction by positioning the adoption of GAI as considering and exploring GAI in K‑12 learning as an educational innovation and the opportunities and limitations for embracing GAI as a tool for learning and teaching.

We have entered a new era of technological innovation with the rapid popularization of artificial intelligence (AI). The access and integration of both predictive and generative artificial intelligence has become widespread with a broad and expanding range of potential applications. While predictive artificial intelligence (PAI) has been mainstreamed for many years (e.g., spelling check in word processing software), generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has been a relatively recent introduction to the general public. Generative artificial intelligence has a wide range of capabilities, including generating text, pictures, images, sounds, voices, and movies, including animation. The breadth of the potential of GAI continues to expand as the accumulation of extant data into repositories increases. The expansion of data accessible for GAI creations has increased the potential usefulness in a wide diversity of educational settings.

We dedicated this special issue of the Journal of Educational Research to research reports on the potential and current applications of GAI in K-12 educational settings. My introductory chapter is intended to provide a roadmap and synthesis for exploring the reports published in this issue detailing the evidence-based practices that include integrating GAI in K-12 education. For this issue, I have curated a diversity of empirical research reports detailing how students and teachers are using GAI to enhance learning and teaching effectiveness. The range of contexts and locations in which the research took place, as detailed in the included reports in this special issue, are a testament to the global use of GAI in K-12 education. Further, the reports reflect how GAI may be transforming teaching and learning in alignment with the activities of 21st-century societies.

## Teacher GAI adoption and instructional use

As with many other education innovations, the adoption of GAI in K-12 for teaching and learning appears to be aligned with the fundamental principles of diffusion theory (Rogers, [Citation 1995](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)). As Nadelson et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) report, there is a wide diversity of justifications and supports for teachers considering (or not considering) GAI for teaching and learning. The association between the adoption and use of GAI with professional development is consistent with the Nadelson and Seifert ([Citation 2016](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) report on teacher embrace and integration of integrated STEM. In their exploration of teacher experiences with GAI, Döğer and Göçen ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) examined the related issues across 15 countries, finding educators tended to maintain a critical perspective on using GAI for teaching and learning. The research provides a unique baseline for future analysis that may focus on the evolution of teachers’ adoption of GAI.

Embracing a similar framework to Nadelson et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)), Isik ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) examined teacher adoption of GAI in alignment with other models of technology and innovation adoption. Isik explored the adoption based on tangible indicators such as usefulness and ease of use among a population of teachers engaged in professional development offerings focused on using GAI for teaching and learning. The research provides empirical documentation for the potential professional development may have on teacher integrations of GAI in their teaching and for their student learning

In their exploration of the perceptions and use of AI tools in eTwinning environments, Döğer and Göçen ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) conducted semi-structured interviews of teachers from a range of participating countries. They found that teachers tended to find benefits to using AI, including increased efficiency in lesson planning, assessing student work, and opportunities for collaboration. Their research also revealed a number of common issues, such as ethical concerns, bias, overreliance, and privacy. Döğer and Göçen also raised concerns about the potential for controlled access to and knowledge of AI to exacerbate social problems, such as broadening the digital divide and supporting AI-driven capitalism. They conclude their report by offering recommendations for evidence-based practices and a roadmap for integrating AI effectively and thoughtfully into teaching and learning.

In their exploration of how teachers perceive and use GAI in teaching foreign languages, Drożdż et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) gathered a combination of qualitative and quantitative data, seeking to empirically document the teachers’ practices. The researchers found the teachers perceived the use of AI-based corpora to be helpful in enhancing their teaching effectiveness and their students’ learning. The teachers noted that the personalization offered by GAI to their students in their language learning was highly beneficial and enhanced student understanding and their acquisition of foreign language. However, nearly half of the teachers in the study indicated they were unfamiliar with using AI to learn languages, suggesting a high potential for emerging uses of GAI in foreign language learning.

To explore how teachers may be using GAI to develop curriculum and learning activities, Delaney et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) conducted a case study research on two high school teachers. Through the lens of a co-design partnership, Delaney et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) examine how teachers learn and subsequently adopt educational innovations, utilizing technology to enhance their practice. Examining how the two teachers were both learning about GAI resources and applications and applying their GAI knowledge to develop curriculum and instructional materials. The researchers found that there is a benefit for teachers to learn about GAI in the context of teaching and learning rather than in a discipline-specific context. In their conclusion, Delaney et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) recognize the need for more research on teacher-generated curriculum and activities, which may be particularly critical as teachers develop more custom instructional materials using GAI.

## Administrators

As leaders in their schools and districts, educational administrators can significantly influence teacher consideration and adoption of educational innovations (e.g., Hsieh et al., [Citation 2024](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)). Given the potential influence, there was high justification for the Göçen and Döğer ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) exploration of how school administrators across 20 countries used GAI in their leadership activities. The adoption of GAI by administrators for their practice will likely influence school policy regarding the use of GAI and teacher integration of GAI into their practice. Furthermore, as Göçen and Döğer discuss, it is also essential to consider the limitations of GAI and maintain a balance with social interactions to achieve effective leadership.

## Elementary education

In their exploration of GAI integration for elementary-level student learning, Tetteh et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) leveraged a culture-techno-contextual approach (CTCA). Students taught using the CTCA method experienced higher learning gains compared to their peers taught using traditional lectures for instruction. Further, the students recognized the affordances of CTCA, which has implications for their use of AI beyond traditional learning conditions. The potential of AI to shift to a more student-centered focus in instruction may be a critical consideration for both research and teaching. As the work of Tetteh et al. suggests, integrating GAI may lead to gains in achieving learning objectives and increased student self-directed learning.

Taking a different approach to using AI-driven vocabulary builders, Temiz and Kafadar ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) compared student gains achieved with the AI software to those obtained using traditional flashcards. The prediction was that using adaptive and generative AI in the computer-based vocabulary builder would enhance student learning in ways superior to using flashcards. The results showed significant short-term gains but no significant differences in the long term as students working with the flashcards performed higher and equivalent on the delayed post-test. The research exemplifies how AI may impact short-term learning compared to traditional methods, but in the long term, some forms of AI-based instruction may not result in significant differences compared to conventional approaches. The research provides a useful model for comparing traditional and AI-based learning and a model for framing AI research in terms of meeting learning objectives rather than achieving superior outcomes.

## Middle school education

As many secondary students have extensive access to the internet (Haidt, [Citation 2024](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) and are likely engaging with GAI for a range of reasons, there is a particular need to explore in depth how secondary students are engaging with GAI in their learning. Adisa and Adefisayo ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) explored how middle school students conceived and perceived GAI should be integrated and used for learning. The students shared perceptions of the importance of teacher supervision of student GAI use and the need to restrict the use of GAI in assessments. The students had mixed preferences for using GAI compared to collaborating with other students. The students’ perspectives offer a unique insight into how students may consider the limitations and ethical uses of GAI, a line of research in which data is collected from teachers or administrators.

Also focusing on using GAI in middle school, Chen et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) explored how the use of GAI could be used to shift history teaching from the common pedagogical model of teacher-led, text-based learning to an approach that is more interactive and personalized for students. Their quasi-experimental design revealed the use of GAI was effective in enhancing student historical knowledge and motivation for learning. The outcome suggests that, when used effectively, GAI can lead to significant learning gains, greater student engagement, and increased creative learning experiences.

## High school education

As students develop, a level of sophistication for learning about and with GAI is likely to increase, as reflected by Smyslova et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)). In their pilot study, they investigated the development of student AI literacy. Focusing on both predictive and generative AI processes, the researchers found significant gains in understanding predictive AI text generation. However, the research also revealed challenges in transitioning their understanding to generative AI processes, with some misconceptions persisting. Further, their research noted gender differences. The research report highlights the importance of moving beyond the mechanics and ethics of GAI use to exploring the actual processes so that students can develop an appreciation of how GAI uses extant data to assemble seemingly unique outputs.

Using the reflective lens of a researcher-practitioner teaching high school history and literature, Wall et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) gathered data to develop a set of evidence-based principles guiding the use of GAI for teaching and learning. Wall et al. moved beyond the approach of limiting student access and trying to control the presence of GAI to a more proactive approach of enhancing students’ GAI literacy. Their proposed principles focus on educating students about GAI, enhancing students’ critical analysis of GAI input and output, and considering student learning holistically. In alignment with their embrace of evidence-based practices, they demonstrate how GAI can enhance student learning.

Extending the empirical documentation of student GAU use, Bieńkowska et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) gathered data from students of different ages, genders, community structures, and schools. The researchers investigated how students used GAI and the impact of GAI use on various variables, including motivation to learn, relationships with teachers, independent thinking, and time management. Bieńkowska and colleagues also examined the students’ perceptions of the advantages and disadvantages of GAI use for learning. They found the students had moderate engagement with GAI and used GAI for a range of tasks. Their research also revealed differences in engagement and motivation for the use of GAI, which were associated with the student’s age, gender, school type, and the community location of the schools the students attended. The results reveal multiple indicators of potential differences in GAI use based on student demographics and expose an array of possible influences that may catalyze the broadening of the digital divide.

Mixing the research on the instructional use of GAI and elements of AI literacy, Liu et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) examined the benefits and limitations of integrating GAI into teaching high school geography. Starting with a comparison of GAI systems in China and the United States, Liu et al. proceed to explore issues related to the accuracy of GAI output, student dependence, ethical use of intellectual property, and equitable access. Thus, while GAI holds the potential for enhancing student geography learning, there are notable limitations that need to be recognized and perhaps resolved to consider GAI as a highly valuable instructional tool.

Moving beyond instructional use and learning using GAI, Meşe et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) explored the critical variable of learning engagement. Using the context of GAI use in learning English, Meşe et al. examined the levels of cognitive, emotional, and behavioral engagement among tenth-grade students who used GAI in a writing course. Their semi-structured interviews revealed evidence of student persistence in seeking feedback and support for correcting errors. The students also engaged in critical thinking, seeking to enhance their writing by identifying and correcting errors in their work. Further, the students’ use reflected elements of curiosity and enjoyment. The research of Meşe et al. underscores the need to move beyond cognitive limitations to include emotional variables as well.

Similar to Meşe et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) focus on English language learners, Woo et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) explored the use of GAI by high school students learning English. In their research, Woo et al. examined how students crafted GAI prompts to create English-language text as part of their writing assignments. The results indicated that students require specific instructions and practice to develop GAI prompts that result in meaningful and useful outputs. The research by Woo et al. reinforces the need for GAI literacy and instruction focused on strategically generating GAI prompts to garner desired and meaningful outcomes.

## Curriculum integration

In a unique study examining the use of GAI as a mechanism for curriculum integration, Kepceoğlu and Oguz-Hacat ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) examined how middle school-level students used GAI to complete assignments that required the students to integrate concepts from mathematics and social studies. In their qualitative exploratory study, Kepceoğlu and Oguz-Hacat found support for using GAI as an instructional context for integrating curriculum. The research found the levels of critical thinking skills of the participating students led to differences in the use and reliance on GAI. The outcomes of the study reflect the potential for using GAI to integrate curriculum and the need to consider and attend to students’ critical thinking skills for meaningful GAI input and their critical examination of GAI output.

## Book review

Closing out this special issue on generative artificial intelligence is a book review by Nufninu et al. ([Citation 2025](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) of _Empowering K-12 Education with AI: Preparing for the Future of Education and Work_ (Chiu, [Citation 2024](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)). The review highlights the focus on GAI for learning and teaching, with many of the ideas well-aligned with the research presented in this issue. In their review, Nufninu et al. emphasize Chiu’s ([Citation 2024](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913#)) primary argument for using GAI as a catalyst for substantial change in K-12 education. As I argued at the beginning of this introduction, GAI is a significant educational innovation that has the potential for a profound impact on teaching and learning. However, as Nufninu et al. also highlight, Chui emphasizes preparing students for a workplace where GAI is integrated as an essential workplace tool.

## Conclusion

Teaching and learning are complex processes that may be constrained by the historical schema of school, limiting the potential for integrating educational innovations. Unlike the introduction of past educational innovations, the presence and use of GAI is impacting nearly all facets of society, business, industry, education, social media, entertainment, sports, and general communication. Given the ubiquitous presence, it will be nearly impossible to stop or even limit the presence of GAI in K-12 education. Thus, rather than trying to prevent or restrict the use of GAI, it is wise we continue to explore and research teaching and learning with the innovation so that we may engage in evidence-based decision-making. The research in this special issue provides a strong foundation for future research on K-12 teaching and learning with GAI.

**Case Study: Lamont (pages 6-9)**

During the summer of 2024, Learner-Centered Collaborative facilitated a three-day Project-Based Learning (PBL) workshop for educators in Lamont who were interested in bringing their unique Learning Model and Portrait of a Learner to life in their classrooms.

Following an introduction to our PBL design elements, this group launched into a yearlong PBL Innovation Cohort where they could brainstorm project ideas, test them out in the classroom, share their results, iterate their designs, and test again. Their design toolbox included Inkwire, a PBL designer that could reference Learner-Centered Collaborative’s PBL design elements, Lamont’s Portrait of a Learner, and Lamont’s Learning Model. This supports educators in their design of projects to ensure they are aligned with district frameworks, strategies, and desired outcomes.

Kelly Williams, Director of Strategic Partnerships and leader of Lamont’s Learner-Centered Innovation Cohort, noted, "Some educators were already using ChatGPT for their project designs, but Inkwire gave them a shortcut. It already had all the district’s foundational documents embedded within the tool and didn’t require special knowledge like “prompt engineering” to receive high-quality output."

With Inkwire, educators can generate project ideas aligned to district-specific standards and learner-centered outcomes, then receive multi-week project plans broken out into daily schedules. That structure doesn’t just save time–it deepens teachers’ understanding of the district’s learner-centered philosophy and how to apply it in practice.

Midway through the cohort experience, 88 percent of participants said they were excited and curious about the role of AI in education, and over 70 percent were using AI tools, including Inkwire, weekly. This frequency of use has helped participants develop an understanding of how to work with AI to get the best results possible.

For instance, Inkwire’s output wasn’t to be taken as 100% complete. “I can look at it and say, okay, day one, yes, I want to do that activity. I’ll skip day two, and I can probably combine days three and four,” said a fifth-grade educator at Alicante Elementary School in Lamont.

She emphasized that her PBL expertise was still needed to assess the quality of Inkwire’s output, but it saved her hours of time upfront creating the initial project plan so she could focus on the finer details of her daily lesson plans.

An important distinction between an application like Inkwire and a Large Language Model (LLM) like ChatGPT is that Inkwire is a one-way experience. With Inkwire, users can choose AI-generated ideas from a dropdown list or provide custom responses based on a preset list of question prompts. Once all answers are added, Inkwire creates a project plan. Compare that to an LLM where users engage in an open conversation, going back and forth, searching for the right things to say that will improve the output.

Antonio Aguilera, a seventh-grade world history educator at Mountain View Middle School, likes to use Inkwire as a brainstorming tool when he’s stumped on what type of project he wants to design that specifically targets one of the competencies that aligns with the district’s Portrait of a Learner.

“With Inkwire, it's easy to just click the dropdown. It's more user-friendly if you're not that tech-savvy. It’s also nice because in ChatGPT, if you forget to directly reference the Lamont Portrait of a Learner in your chat, then your results might be too generic, whereas with Inkwire, that's a non-issue because it's already integrated.” This points to the value of a tool that is pre-trained with district frameworks and materials as references.

Both Lamont educators mentioned taking advantage of what each tool does best. During the 2024-25 academic year, Inkwire’s strength was designing competency-aligned project plans, whereas an LLM like ChatGPT was a better thought partner for lesson plan design.

After receiving her project plan from Inkwire, a fifth-grade educator inserted it into ChatGPT and asked questions like: “Can you suggest what you would put on each slide for this topic? Can you give me a list of women who are in STEM? Can you make sure this is for fifth-grade students?”

Shortly after the year wrapped up, Inkwire released a new feature that provides educators with individual lesson plans and suggests detailed activities. This is a great addition, but it doesn’t make the educators’ use of ChatGPT irrelevant. There continues to be great value in stacking different AI tools together and taking advantage of what each does best.

“Inkwire is like your coach. It’s prompting you with these questions that train you to internalize this learner-centered mindset. The more I’m internalizing those questions for myself, the more I start to see teaching and learning through those questions more broadly,” -Kelly Williams

This cohort experience gave educators a new way to see themselves as teachers and learners. Going into the summer and the 2025-26 academic year, educators are excited to continue the journey and are already planning what projects they might try next.

During the final Celebration of Learning in May 2025, Lamont’s Innovation Cohort participants talked about how they saw themselves as learners throughout the experience. Many agreed with the sentiment shared by one participant about readiness: “I wasn’t fully ready to try PBL or work with an AI tool. I didn’t have it all mapped out. I just gave myself permission to try and learn along the way.” That willingness to try without knowing how everything would play out translated to a new relationship with students where educators can say, “I’m learning alongside you. We’re in this together.”

**Case Study: Escondido (pages 10-13)**

Escondido Union School District (EUSD) had already done the hard and foundational work of building a Framework for the Future: A Portrait of a Learner was in place, a Learning Model was in use, and educators were beginning to test learner-centered strategies in classrooms.

With so much change already happening, introducing a new technology like AI felt like a stretch. However, for North Broadway Elementary Principal Cherry Moore, she could already see this technology wasn't going to wait for anyone. Students and classroom educators were already tinkering with it on their own, so it was imperative to create space for open dialogue and experimentation.

Rather than launching AI broadly, the school partnered with Learner-Centered Collaborative in spring 2025 and formed a Design Team of innovative educators who were excited to put AI to the test.

Their primary tool for experimentation was the Learning Experience Accelerator (LEA) App, developed using Playlab. This application is a learning experience thought partner trained using Learner-Centered Collaborative’s research-based Learning Model and classroom strategies as well as Escondido’s Learner Profile competencies. It helps educators integrate those competencies and strategies into their daily instruction aligned to desired outcomes.

When educators began playing with the tool, “They all were like, 'wow, I can see this unlocking our teachers,'" recalled César Morales, Partner Lead for Escondido Union School District.

The Learning Experience Accelerator seamlessly integrates the district's unique Portrait of a Learner competencies and Learning Model, state standards, and LCC's learner-centered strategies so that the output is consistently aligned with the district's implementation goals.

When using the tool, educators answer questions about their grade level and describe a unit, project, or lesson they are planning to teach. The app then connects their idea to specific Portrait of a Learner competencies and shares success criteria based on their grade band. It also provides concrete strategies for explicitly teaching the relevant skills, providing feedback to learners, and designing opportunities for learners to demonstrate and reflect on the skills throughout the unit or project.

Notably, while the EUSD Design Team of early adopters was experimenting with the app, every educator in the school was building a knowledge base around the district's Framework for the Future.

"We had done some work with the district's new Learning Model (developed in collaboration with Learner-Centered Collaborative), so we had this foundation," reflected Cherry. "Then we started asking teachers to create a learning experience based on what they understood about the Learning Model to see if what they designed could produce the Whole-Learner Outcomes expressed in our district's Portrait of a Learner." Cherry felt it was imperative to develop this foundational knowledge prior to introducing the LEA app so educators could confidently assess and iterate on the outputs.

Once the foundation was in place throughout the school and the Design Team felt confident about how to get the most out of Playlab, the bot was introduced at an all-staff meeting where 5th-grade educator Katie Taylor demonstrated how to use the tool to rework an existing lesson.

Her colleagues watched as she selected relevant learner outcomes from their Portrait, received suggestions aligned to their Learning Model, and adapted the ideas to meet her classroom needs. The live demo was catalytic. “The tool builds confidence and has educators saying 'oh my gosh, I know more than I thought I knew about our Portrait and Learning Model,'" César shared. "This tool just elevates those connections for teachers."

“I think by August, we will be in a place where teachers will take a fresh look at the plans they made, go in and identify what Whole-Learner Outcomes their plans will hit, and then explore how students might self-assess based on the Whole-Learner Outcomes they’re developing. I feel like that’s when our teachers are going to be more energized and ready to have more tools to help them do that work.” -Cherry Moore

As they head into the summer and plan for the 2025-26 academic year, the emphasis will be on seeing the Learning Experience Accelerator App as a way to enhance unit planning and build capacity for designing Learner Profile aligned learning experiences.

North Broadway’s story shows that scaling AI use isn’t about urgency—it’s about strategy. With a clear vision, phased rollout, peer modeling, and purposeful tools, the school created conditions where innovation could grow without top-down mandates, but rather with authentic buy-in from educators.

**Conclusion (page 14)**

The stories from Lamont and Escondido remind us that AI is not a shortcut or a substitute for educator expertise—it’s a tool. When integrated within a clear and shared vision like a Framework for the Future, AI helps educators navigate the complexity of learner-centered models and translate big ideas into meaningful day-to-day practice. Tools like Inkwire and Playlab don’t replace professional judgment; they elevate it.

Change in education is not just about adopting new models; it’s about building the capacity of educators to implement them effectively. AI-enabled tools provide educators with specific ideas for bringing the Portrait of a Learner competencies into their daily lessons, units, and projects while implementing learner-centered strategies. These tools not only enhance learning design but also foster continuous professional learning and collaboration.

### Four essential personalized learning practices before using artificial intelligence

Before incorporating AI into co-designing curriculum, instruction or classroom routines, educators agreed that four core personalized learning practices should already be in place:

1.   **Designing for variability:** recognizing that students come with different experiences, strengths and needs and that personalized learning begins by honoring where each learner starts and designing appropriate learning pathways for success
2.   **Establishing classrooms that support agency and independence:**creating and modeling clear procedures and co-created expectations so that learners know how to navigate tasks and engage in independent problem-solving as active participants in their learning
3.   **Cultivating student ownership:**reflecting on practice and adjusting instruction to create space for students to make decisions about their learning; this requires flexibility and a willingness to release control in support of student ownership
4.   **Designing with purpose:** clarifying learning goals and criteria with learners, using those targets to guide instructional decisions and thoughtfully considering differentiation and agency when designing learning experiences

### Four core personalized learning beliefs for an AI-enabled classroom

Conversations with educators surfaced a shared set of assumptions necessary for AI to meaningfully amplify personalized learning.

1.   **Learning is human-centered, not tool-driven.**AI should serve personalization while reinforcing, not replacing, strong instruction, human thinking and the relationships that make learning matter.
2.   **Digital literacy is essential**. Educators must be able to guide and refine AI use rather than outsourcing instructional decisions to technology.
3.   **Process over product.** Teachers believe all students can learn and grow over time and design learning experiences that prioritize growth, reflection and continuous improvement.
4.   **Human judgment remains paramount**. Educators must check outputs to ensure accuracy and preserve the integrity of instruction.

Starting an AI journey with these norms in mind ensures that the work starts from a place that is aligned to the purpose of personalized learning.

### Emerging themes: how artificial intelligence can support personalized learning

As educators explored practical, meaningful ways AI can support personalized learning, six themes surfaced as a clear throughline across perspectives.

#### 1. Assessment and feedback

AI can strengthen assessment and feedback by making results more immediate and actionable. Educators shared that AI has helped them to quickly identify what students understand and where they need additional support, while also creating meaningful checkpoints that inform their instructional decisions. Leveled skill assessments, especially for reading comprehension, where questions can be directly aligned to standards, can improve accuracy and consistency. When used with intentionality, AI shifts assessments and feedback from time-consuming tasks into dynamic tools that support learning and growth.

#### 2. Data-informed decision making

AI can enhance educators’ ability to turn complex data into clear next steps for instructional design. Teachers spoke about using AI to analyze state assessment results, summarize large sets of student work and performance artifacts and revise lesson plans based on emerging trends. AI can provide educators with advanced analytics and reporting to support collaboration, data-informed decision making and progress monitoring. Because AI simplifies the data analysis process, educators can focus their time and energy on interpretation and action rather than data management.

#### 3. Engagement and relevance

AI helps to bring learning to life by connecting instruction to students’ interests and experiences. Teachers described using AI to hyper-personalize content based on learner preferences. Gamifying lessons through simulations or role-playing opportunities and providing alternative formats for students who are less comfortable speaking aloud are a few of the examples provided. AI can support student choice, bring new concepts to life through real-world scenarios and deliver instant, adaptive feedback that can keep learners motivated. Together, these uses contribute to learning environments where students feel engaged and genuinely curious.

#### 4. Student agency

AI is a powerful support for building student ownership of learning. Educators have used it to design standards-aligned choice boards and personalized learning pathways that connect directly to clear goals and success criteria. Whether through flexible structures, project options or other forms, AI makes it easier to offer learners choice for how they will demonstrate understanding. By helping visualize skill progressions and learning growth, AI can support transparency and put students in a position to monitor their own progress. With AI as a partner, teachers can create learning experiences where choice and ownership are the norm.

#### 5. Planning and instructional design

AI can support instructional planning by enhancing creativity, like generating innovative and standards-aligned project ideas, while reducing the time spent on routine tasks. Teachers found it valuable for co-designing lessons, essential questions and success criteria, as well as streamlining formatting, grammar and revisions. AI can also help with pacing unit plans or condensing content when time is limited. It also supports technical needs such as coding for Canvas or Canva. Used this way, AI expands what’s possible in planning while keeping educators firmly in the driver’s seat.

#### 6. Differentiation

Differentiation becomes more manageable and more natural with the support of AI. Teachers use it to generate questions that deepen critical thinking, level texts across Lexile ranges and increase rigor for advanced learners. AI also helps educators embed accommodations directly into curriculum for students with IEPs, 504 plans, BIPs and multilingual needs. By quickly providing multimodal and multilingual content, AI allows educators to design learning experiences that balance access and challenge, while assisting with progress monitoring and translation.

# AIGC in K–12 Classrooms: A Global Research Report on Practical Applications, Frameworks, and Future Directions

**Date:** August 2026  
**Expert Role:** K–12 Education Researcher & Frontline Teacher

---

## Executive Summary

Artificial Intelligence–Generated Content (AIGC) has moved from an experimental novelty to a permanent, rapidly scaling presence in primary and secondary education worldwide. By mid-2026, 86% of education organizations globally use generative AI—the highest adoption rate of any industry (Microsoft, 2025). 92% of U.S. K–12 students report using AI tools, and 83% of teachers use generative AI for lesson planning, feedback, or content support (RAND, 2025; Third Rock Techkno, 2025). This report synthesizes findings from over 30 peer-reviewed studies, dozens of district-level case studies, and international policy analyses to provide a comprehensive, actionable framework for understanding and implementing AIGC in K–12 classrooms.

---

## 1. Overall Framework: AIGC Integration in K–12 Education

The global landscape of AIGC in K–12 education can be organized into a **Three-Domain Framework** that captures both the purpose and the locus of use:

| Domain | Focus | Primary Users | Key Functions |
|--------|-------|---------------|---------------|
| **Teacher Efficiency & Instructional Design** | Reducing workload, accelerating planning | Teachers | Lesson planning, assessment creation, differentiation, IEP drafting, content adaptation |
| **Student Learning & Personalization** | Enhancing outcomes, engagement, agency | Students | AI tutoring, adaptive content, feedback, creative exploration, self-regulated learning |
| **System & Operational Management** | Streamlining administration, informing policy | Administrators, leaders | Policy agents, communication automation, data analytics, procurement oversight |

Within each domain, AIGC applications fall into **five functional categories**:

1. **Content Generation** – Creating text, images, quizzes, rubrics, slide decks, and multimedia.
2. **Adaptive & Personalized Instruction** – Tailoring pacing, difficulty, and modality to individual learners.
3. **Assessment & Feedback** – Automated grading, formative check-ins, instant feedback loops.
4. **Tutoring & Scaffolding** – AI-powered conversational agents, customized chatbots, project coaches.
5. **Administrative & Operational Automation** – IEP/504 plan drafting, policy retrieval, communication drafting, sentiment analysis.

---

## 2. Detailed Category Discussions with Global Case Studies

### 2.1 Teacher Efficiency & Instructional Design

**Category 1: AI-Assisted Lesson Planning**

This is the most widespread AIGC use globally. A RAND survey (2025) found 71% of U.S. teachers use AI for lesson planning, and 68% use it for creating quizzes and assessments. Purpose-built tools like **MagicSchoolAI**, **Eduaide.AI**, **SchoolAI**, **Brisk Teaching**, and **Curipod** embed curriculum standards and support differentiated outputs.

*Case Example – Lamont Elementary School District (California, USA):*  
During the 2024–25 academic year, Lamont launched a yearlong PBL Innovation Cohort using **Inkwire**, an AI tool pre-loaded with the district’s Portrait of a Learner and Learning Model. Educators generated multi-week project plans aligned to district-specific competencies and standards. Midway through the cohort, 88% of participants were excited about AI, and over 70% used AI tools weekly. A fifth-grade teacher reported, “I can look at it and say, okay, day one, yes, I want to do that activity. I’ll skip day two, and I can probably combine days three and four.” The combination of Inkwire for project design and ChatGPT for lesson-level detail produced a “stacking” approach that saved hours while preserving professional judgment.  
**Source:** [Learner-Centered Collaborative Case Study PDF](https://learnercentered.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/AI-case-study.pdf)

*Case Example – Sixth-Grade Science Differentiation (USA):*  
A teacher used an AI curriculum generator to create three versions of a science text—one at grade level, one simplified for struggling readers, and one translated into Spanish for ELL students—in 15 minutes instead of two hours.  
**Source:** [SchoolAI Blog](https://schoolai.com/blog/ai-curriculum-generator)

**Category 2: Special Education and IEP/504 Plan Automation**

Special education teachers face intense administrative burdens, with IEP documents often stretching to 50 pages and 70% of U.S. public schools reporting special education teacher vacancies (2023–24). AI tools are providing critical relief.

*Case Example – Streamline Platform (USA):*  
In July 2025, Sanford-based Better Speech introduced **Streamline**, an AI-powered platform for managing special education. IEP preparation time dropped by 90%, from 3 hours to 10 minutes. Speech-language pathology teams also reported improved therapy efficiency.  
**Source:** [RAISE Summit AI Case Studies](https://www.raisesummit.com/post/ai-case-studies-education)

*Case Example – Lopez Island School District (Washington, USA):*  
In early 2026, special education teacher Rose Prust used **Magic School** and **Ablespace** to refine IEP goals. AI analysis of interaction data revealed that a student with cortical visual impairment responded better to auditory cues than visual ones. The IEP was revised to prioritize multi-sensory instruction, resulting in improved cause-and-effect comprehension within one week.  
**Source:** [RAISE Summit AI Case Studies](https://www.raisesummit.com/post/ai-case-studies-education)

**Category 3: Operational AI for School Administration**

*Case Example – Westport Public Schools (Connecticut, USA):*  
Westport developed three custom AI agents: a **Virtual Board of Education agent** trained on years of board meeting videos to help staff anticipate questions and refine materials; a **Communication agent** that automates press releases and analyzes social media sentiment; and a **Policy agent** trained on district policy manuals and state statutes to locate requirements and draft policy-aligned documents. All agents operate with human oversight.  
**Source:** [Hanover Research](https://www.hanoverresearch.com/insights-blog/k-12-education/developing-k-12-ai-literacy-for-your-district)

---

### 2.2 Student Learning & Personalization

**Category 4: AI Tutors and Adaptive Learning Platforms**

*Case Example – South Korea’s Nationwide AI Tutor Rollout:*  
South Korea has undertaken a nationwide deployment of AI tutors offering both academic and emotional support. The model is being closely scrutinized for its positive effects on learner engagement and for gaps in transferability to other contexts.  
**Source:** [FifthRow Global Policies Analysis](https://fifthrow.com/blog/ai-in-k-12-education-global-policies-outcomes-and-actionable-best-practices)

*Case Example – SchoolAI Spaces (Multiple U.S. Districts):*  
SchoolAI’s **Spaces** feature allows teachers to create customizable AI tutor environments—for example, a Shakespeare discussion guide, a math problem explainer, or an interactive Choose Your Own Adventure exploration of the Revolutionary War. Students interact one-on-one with the AI, and teachers can view transcripts to identify misconceptions.  
**Source:** [Edutopia](https://www.edutopia.org/article/using-ai-generate-lesson-ideas)

**Category 5: Student-Centered Creative and Critical Thinking with AI**

*Case Example – Middle School Midjourney Workshop:*  
A three-workshop intervention (3 hours each, over 3 weeks) introduced middle school students to AI through image generation. After learning about web scraping, datasets, and prompt crafting, students used **Midjourney** in small teams to generate images collaboratively. The approach built AI literacy, creativity, and critical analysis of AI outputs.  
**Source:** [Frontiers Systematic Review](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/education/articles/10.3389/feduc.2025.1647573/full)

*Case Example – High School History with GAI (Chen et al., 2025):*  
A quasi-experimental study in middle school history used generative AI to shift from teacher-led, text-based learning to interactive, personalized instruction. Results showed significant gains in historical knowledge, student motivation, and creative learning experiences.  
**Source:** [Journal of Educational Research Special Issue](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913)

*Case Example – High School English Learners and Prompt Crafting (Woo et al., 2025):*  
High school students learning English used GAI to create English-language text for writing assignments. Findings revealed that students require explicit instruction and practice in crafting effective prompts to generate meaningful, useful outputs. The research reinforces the need for dedicated GAI literacy instruction.  
**Source:** [Journal of Educational Research Special Issue](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913)

**Category 6: Personalized Learning and Differentiation**

*Case Example – Escondido Union School District (California, USA):*  
Escondido formed a Design Team in spring 2025 to pilot the **Learning Experience Accelerator (LEA) App**, built on Playlab. The tool was trained on the district’s Learner Profile competencies and Learning Model. Teachers answered questions about a planned unit, and the app connected their ideas to specific competencies, success criteria, and strategies for teaching and assessing those skills. A live demo by a fifth-grade teacher was catalytic: colleagues saw how the tool “elevates connections” between their existing knowledge and the district’s framework.  
**Source:** [Learner-Centered Collaborative Case Study PDF](https://learnercentered.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/AI-case-study.pdf)

## 3. Practical Implementation Methods

### 3.1 Foundational Conditions for Success

Based on an analysis of successful implementations, four conditions must be in place before introducing AIGC tools:

1. **Clear Shared Vision** – A “Portrait of a Learner” and a Learning Model that articulate desired outcomes for the whole child. Tools like Inkwire and the LEA App are most effective when they reference district-specific frameworks.  
   **Source:** [Learner-Centered Collaborative Case Study](https://learnercentered.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/AI-case-study.pdf); [Hanover Research](https://www.hanoverresearch.com/insights-blog/k-12-education/developing-k-12-ai-literacy-for-your-district)

2. **Human-Centered Pedagogy** – AI should serve, not replace, strong instruction. As KnowledgeWorks educators emphasize, “Learning is human-centered, not tool-driven.”  
   **Source:** [KnowledgeWorks](https://knowledgeworks.org/resources/artificial-intelligence-optimize-personalized-learning)

3. **Digital Literacy and AI Literacy Foundations** – Students and teachers need explicit instruction in prompt crafting, evaluating AI outputs, and understanding bias, privacy, and ethics.  
   **Source:** [Journal of Educational Research Special Issue](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00220671.2025.2514913); [Day of AI Curriculum](https://dayofai.org/curriculum-resources)

4. **Human-in-the-Loop Oversight** – All outputs must be reviewed by educators. A first-grade teacher does not magically become a “prompt engineer”; professional judgment remains paramount.  
   **Source:** [Hanover Research](https://www.hanoverresearch.com/insights-blog/k-12-education/developing-k-12-ai-literacy-for-your-district); [PanoramaEd](https://www.panoramaed.com/blog/generative-ai-in-education)

### 3.2 Phased Implementation Roadmap

| Phase | Actions | Timeline | Key Metrics |
|-------|---------|----------|-------------|
| **1. Readiness Assessment** | Audit infrastructure, policies, staff AI literacy; survey stakeholders | 1–3 months | Baseline AI literacy scores; readiness checklist (e.g., CoSN Gen AI Maturity Tool) |
| **2. Vision & Policy Co-creation** | Develop shared AI vision, flexible policies, ethical guardrails | 2–3 months | Policy adoption rate; stakeholder buy-in |
| **3. Pilot with Early Adopters** | Form a Design Team of 5–15 educators; provide 1–2 tools, low-stakes practice time | 3–6 months | % of teachers using AI weekly; qualitative feedback |
| **4. Peer Modeling & Scaling** | Live demos in staff meetings; share success stories; expand tool access | 6–12 months | % of teachers trained; reduction in planning time |
| **5. Systemwide Integration** | Embed AI literacy across curriculum; establish feedback loops; update policies annually | 12–24 months | Student engagement metrics; teacher retention; equity indicators |

**Source:** Synthesized from [Hanover Research](https://www.hanoverresearch.com/insights-blog/k-12-education/developing-k-12-ai-literacy-for-your-district); [Leading Educators](https://leadingeducators.org/generative-practice); [PanoramaEd](https://www.panoramaed.com/blog/generative-ai-in-education); [Learner-Centered Collaborative](https://learnercentered.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/AI-case-study.pdf)

### 3.3 Professional Development That Works

90% of reviewed studies emphasize the need for teacher professional development for AI-integrated classrooms (Frontiers, 2025). Effective PD is:

- **Job-embedded and workflow-anchored** – Teachers learn by using AI on tasks they already do: lesson planning, creating assessments, drafting communications.
- **Low-stakes and exploratory** – Educators need “permission to try” without fear of failure. Lamont’s cohort gave educators “permission to try and learn along the way.”
- **Peer-led and collaborative** – The Escondido case showed that a live teacher demo was more effective than top-down training.
- **Ongoing, not one-shot** – Westport’s success with custom AI agents required continuous iteration and training.

**Source:** [Hanover Research](https://www.hanoverresearch.com/insights-blog/k-12-education/developing-k-12-ai-literacy-for-your-district); [Leading Educators](https://leadingeducators.org/generative-practice); [PanoramaEd](https://www.panoramaed.com/blog/generative-ai-in-education)

## 4. Future Trends (2026–2030)

### 4.1 From General AI to Specialized Educational Intelligence

The market is shifting from generic chatbots toward purpose-built K–12 AI tools with embedded standards alignment, FERPA/COPPA compliance, and district-specific customization. The global AI education market is projected to grow from $7.05 billion (2025) to $136.79 billion by 2035 (CAGR ~35%).  
**Source:** [Engageli AI Statistics](https://www.engageli.com/blog/ai-in-education-statistics); [SchoolAI](https://schoolai.com/blog/ai-curriculum-generator)

### 4.2 Personalization at Scale

AI-driven adaptive learning is moving from pilot to practice. By 2026, 74% of U.S. school districts have provided AI training for teachers (RAND, 2025). The OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026 confirms that GenAI can support learning when guided by clear teaching principles, but warns that “outsourcing tasks to GenAI” without pedagogical support does not produce real learning gains.  
**Source:** [OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/oecd-digital-education-outlook-2026_062a7394-en.html)

### 4.3 AI Literacy as a Core Competency

Initiatives like **Day of AI** (MIT RAISE) reached over 2 million students across 175 countries in 2025, and AI literacy is increasingly embedded in national curricula. China’s mandatory K–12 AI curriculum and the proliferation of free curricula (e.g., TeachAI, AI4K12) signal that AI literacy is becoming a foundational skill.  
**Source:** [Day of AI](https://dayofai.org/curriculum-resources); [FifthRow](https://fifthrow.com/blog/ai-in-k-12-education-global-policies-outcomes-and-actionable-best-practices); [AI4K12](https://ai4k12.org/resources/list-of-resources)

### 4.4 Regulatory Fragmentation and Ethical Guardrails

No national bans on AI in K–12 education have been enacted since 2025, but targeted restrictions exist (e.g., New York’s ban on facial recognition, West Virginia’s limits on GenAI for assignments). Only 33 U.S. states have issued official AI guidance. The need for standardized cross-national metrics, data protection, and algorithmic transparency remains urgent.  
**Source:** [FifthRow](https://fifthrow.com/blog/ai-in-k-12-education-global-policies-outcomes-and-actionable-best-practices); [US Department of Education AI Report](https://www.ed.gov/sites/ed/files/documents/ai-report/ai-report.pdf)

### 4.5 Equity and the Digital Divide

One-third of humanity remains offline, and access to cutting-edge AI models is unequally distributed. The **OECD Digital Education Outlook** and **UNESCO** both emphasize that AI risks widening existing gaps unless infrastructure investment, linguistic adaptation, and culturally responsive design are prioritized.  
**Source:** [UNESCO](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/ai-and-future-education-disruptions-dilemmas-and-directions); [OECD](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/oecd-digital-education-outlook-2026_062a7394-en.html)

### 4.6 Emerging Research Gaps

The Frontiers systematic review (2025) identifies critical gaps: few studies examine early childhood education, special needs, rural contexts, or non-English-speaking regions. Only two of 30 reviewed studies examined self-regulated learning with GenAI. Longitudinal studies on long-term impacts on creativity, critical thinking, and equity remain scarce.  
**Source:** [Frontiers Systematic Review](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/education/articles/10.3389/feduc.2025.1647573/full)

## 5. Recommendations for Educators

### 5.1 For Classroom Teachers

1. **Start small, with one repetitive task.** Pick one thing—differentiating a reading passage, generating a quiz, drafting a parent email—and use a purpose-built AI tool for that task. Review, adjust, and iterate.
2. **Stack tools strategically.** Use Inkwire for project design and ChatGPT for lesson-level details, as Lamont teachers did. Each tool has strengths; know when to use which.
3. **Teach AI literacy explicitly.** Students need to learn how to craft effective prompts, evaluate AI outputs for bias and accuracy, and understand when AI is helpful and when it is not.
4. **Always maintain human judgment.** AI is a co-pilot, not the pilot. Verify all outputs, adapt them to your students’ contexts, and never outsource pedagogical decisions.
5. **Collaborate and share.** Join or form a cohort of early adopters, as in Lamont and Escondido. Peer modeling and shared learning are more effective than isolated experimentation.

### 5.2 For School and District Leaders

1. **Co-create a shared AI vision** with staff, students, families, and community members. Ground it in your district’s Portrait of a Learner and existing frameworks.
2. **Adopt a flexible, evolving AI policy** that addresses responsible use, data privacy, ethics, and academic integrity. Update it annually.
3. **Invest in ongoing, job-embedded professional development.** Provide low-stakes time for teachers to explore tools, and use peer-led demonstrations to build confidence.
4. **Prioritize equity.** Ensure that AI tools are accessible to all students, including those with disabilities, multilingual learners, and students in under-resourced schools. Invest in infrastructure and culturally responsive content.
5. **Choose purpose-built, compliant tools.** Evaluate AI vendors for FERPA/COPPA compliance, data security (SOC 2), built-in standards alignment, and transparent data practices.
6. **Establish feedback loops.** Regularly survey teachers and students on AI use, measure impact on learning outcomes and engagement, and use data to refine implementation.

### 5.3 For Policymakers and Researchers

1. **Develop standardized cross-national metrics** for AI impact in K–12 education, including equity indicators.
2. **Fund longitudinal studies** on the long-term effects of AIGC on creativity, critical thinking, self-regulated learning, and social-emotional development.
3. **Invest in non-English AI resources** and culturally grounded curricula to ensure global relevance.
4. **Create clear, enforceable guardrails** for algorithmic transparency, data privacy, and human oversight, without stifling innovation.
5. **Support teacher preparation programs** that embed AI literacy and human-AI collaboration as core competencies.

## 6. Conclusion

AIGC is not a passing trend in K–12 education; it is a structural shift that is already reshaping how teachers plan, how students learn, and how schools operate. The evidence from global case studies—from Lamont and Escondido in California, to Westport in Connecticut, to national pilots in Iceland, South Korea, and China—demonstrates that the most successful implementations share a common DNA: they are grounded in a clear vision of learner outcomes, driven by human relationships, supported by ongoing professional learning, and guided by ethical guardrails.

The polarizing debate—AI as savior versus AI as threat—is unproductive. The real challenge is not whether to use AI, but how to use it wisely, equitably, and in service of the deeper goals of education: fostering curiosity, critical thinking, creativity, and human connection. As Ana Lucía Pérez, a 10th-grade student from Puerto Rico, observed at the 2025 MIT AI and Education Summit: *“Change doesn’t start with perfection. It starts with curiosity and courage.”*
